blocks.text: Rectus Abdominis (Abs) - Spinal Flexion/Posterior Pelvic Tilt
Synergists:
External Obliques - Spinal Flexion
Transverse Abdominis - Hollowing (supports abdominal wall)
Pelvic Floor (in coordination with TA) - Pelvis stabilization
Rectus Femoris (Rec Fem) - Hip Flexion
Psoas -Hip Flexion
Considerations for setup:

The weight stack should be set prior to the client entering. A standard gap of 6 will most likely be used although this may vary from machine to machine and will be decided by the location’s Studio Leader and MSF Corporate.

Ensure the movement arm (roller pad) is in the upright and locked position. The movement arm will only rest in the forward position. While it can be pushed back (away from the weight stack) it will not stay in that position. The instructor needs to take extra precaution in controlling the position of the movement arm throughout the set and especially during entry/exit.

Determine height of the seat pad, by having the client palpate and point to the iliac crest (point of the hip). This should align approximately with the level of the roller pad at the back of the seat. This is the theoretical alignment for this exercise. In theory, this will optimally align the axis of rotation of the machine with the axis of rotation of the body, near the top of the pelvis. See the following point for the practical alignment considerations.

From a practical standpoint, the instructor should still take into consideration the height of the subject and/or the relative size of the hip girdle and surrounding tissues. In either case, there is a possibility where there will be a substantial shift in the center of gravity, giving the subject more mass above the movement arm of the machine. They become more top heavy in a sense. This will create additional leverage that does not come from the targeted musculature and can lead to a false sense of progression. As a result, there is a likelihood that the subject will require more weight, simultaneously making the exercise less effective with more risk.

So yes, the theoretical alignment of having the top of the iliac crest in line with the top of the roller pad will be the best starting point. It will also often be the most optimal setting. The point here is that the instructor needs to be attentive to the size and proportion of each individual client in making the final determination in a practical sense.

The next consideration is the foot placement on the fixed footplate. This will determine the knee angle that we are trying to match to the angle of the femur restraint (knee pad). Ensure the femur restraint is unwound and moved away from the seat to allow room for the client to enter.

Alert client to the movement arm to ensure that they do not run into it while entering the seat. Instructor should keep the movement arm (roller pad) in the locked position during entry/exit and move it to the rearmost position. The instructor will have to HOLD THE MOVEMENT ARM IN THIS POSITION AS IT WILL FALL FORWARD IF NOT SECURED.

The feet should be located so that when the feet are placed on the platform the angle of the knee is approximately congruent to the angle of the femur restraint. This will result in the pads sitting flush against the tibia and femur.

With the foot placement established, the femur restraint should be positioned and tightened down so that the pads basically straddle the knees evenly (i.e. the patella should be approximately centered in the opening between the two pad, with one pad sitting above the knee on the femur and the other resting below the knee along the tibia).
The pads should be snug enough to allow a little bit of wiggle room against the leg but not enough that there is a space or gap.

With the lower body secure, the next step will be to unlock the movement arm (roller pad) and carefully lower it into position. Instruct the client to lean back and be ready for the roller pad to pass in front of their face. As this happens, the client should lift their arms up and over the top of the roller pad so that it sits in their armpits or as close as they can comfortably get it. Have the client bring their elbows closer together and place their hands up in front of their head in a “prayer” position.

This movement will start at the upper turnaround in the contracted position. The instructor will assist the movement arm and client down to this point. Standing behind the client and grabbing the movement arm instruct the client to curl down and tighten their abdomen as you push the movement arm forward and down to reach this position.
Posture/Get Set:

This exercise requires an interpersonal transfer of the load where the client will increase their effort (“tighten down your abdominals”) while the instructor gradually releases their effort so that the movement arm is kept stationary in the contracted position. Importantly the instructor should always be in control and provide direction to the client in these types of transfers. The instructor will assist the movement arm (and client) into the contracted position and there should be an indicating cue, something to the effect of “that…iiiisss…yours” as the weight is transferred.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:
ECCENTRIC: Once the movement arm is transferred, instruct the client to “slowly begin to uncurl their spine from the bottom up as they begin to lower the weight”.

As the client is lowering the weight, the instructor should provide the necessary instruction as to when to change directions. This will happen when the weights touch in the lower turnaround. So prior to reaching this point, instruct the client to “uncurl far enough to allow the weights to barely touch before changing directions and curling back down.”  Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of any exercise.

LOWER TURNAROUND: Once the subject reaches the lower turnaround (i.e. weights touch), they will “immediately” or “continuously” or “seamlessly” change directions. (Importantly, ‘immediate’ means right away, but does not mean suddenly in this case).

CONCENTRIC:  After a continuous change of direction, the client will “begin to curl back down one vertebrae at a time from the top down toward their lap (or hip crease)” or “begin to draw their rib cage down to their pelvis”. As the client makes their way through the concentric portion of the first rep, it is helpful to describe the anatomical action that is expected. Something along the lines of “tighten your abdominals and round your back…”

UPPER TURNAROUND: The upper turnaround will be when the subject has fully contracted their abdomen. Not necessarily when the movement arm reaches the top of their legs. It is important to teach clients that it is not always the goal to move the movement arm through its fullest excursion possible. Instead the movement should cease when the targeted musculature is fully contracted, which may come before the machine’s movement arm has been moved to its furthest point possible.

At the instant the subject reaches the end stop there should be a brief pause in the contracted position (and a 2 to 3 second “squeeze” from the third rep on). This is unlike our compound pushing movements (LP, CP, OH, SD) where the upper turnaround is met with continuous change of direction into the eccentric phase. This brief pause and slightly longer squeeze require an additional level of focus and control, making the movement safer. They also afford the subject an opportunity to “feel” the target muscles.

Verbiage on a squeeze might be “keep rounding, keep breathing, [click], ease out” or “tighten down hard, trying to cramp your abdominals, [click], ease out.” Keep in mind we need to teach the client HOW to squeeze. Saying “squeeze” alone is not a useful instruction. The MSF Exercise Practitioner is constantly teaching!
NOTES

It is our company policy that we ascertain any and all limitations and/or contraindications to resistance training for all of our clients and determine which movement patterns these may affect. This is one of the primary purposes of having the prospective client complete the consultation paperwork. It is also a primary purpose of the consultation itself, to understand the limitations of each individual and to tailor the workouts accordingly. There will be certain subjects that do not tolerate lumbar flexion from an orthopedic standpoint. For these individuals it may make sense to omit the abdominal (trunk flexion) movement pattern altogether until they have medical clearance or a better understanding of the diagnosis if they do not already have one.

While avoiding the movement pattern altogether would be the most conservative approach overall, we may be able to actually help the client by strengthening the area. For those with no underlying orthopedic issue, the most conservative approach would be to perform a Timed Static Contraction (TSC). In this situation, the instructor would pin a heavy enough weight so that the movement arm cannot be moved (i.e. too heavy to actually lift). Then, with the client properly secured in the seat, the instructor will position the movement arm to some approximate midpoint in the range of motion, maybe slightly biased toward the upper turnaround (i.e. contracted position). The instructor would then lead the client through an increasing STATIC effort against the roller pad. This is typically a 50% effort for 30 seconds, a 75% effort for another 30 seconds, and a final 30 seconds at an all out effort, for a total of 90 seconds of continuous effort. This approach when followed at least weekly for months at a time can build an appreciable level of strength contributing to improved function of the involved muscles. There also tends to be a carryover effect to what has been estimated at 15 degrees in either direction of the position of the static exercise. There is also a possibility that the client will be able to one day perform the abdominal exercise dynamically and continue to progress.

If the TSC arrangement discussed above is not possible, there may be a good chance that the subject can tolerate the Torso Rotation exercise. By performing this exercise, there will be a benefit to the abdominal muscles while avoiding the discomfort of the trunk flexion movement pattern.

The resistance profile on the abdominal machine makes it heavier at the lower turnaround and lighter in the contracted position. This makes sense as we are biomechanically weaker in the contracted position. Because of this however, the contracted position can become a point of respite for subjects that are relying on their instincts and looking for relief. In this case, it may be useful to place a selector pin into one of the upper holes of the stack pin (above the weight stack). This will create an end stop and essentially truncate the most contracted of this exercise. If this strategy is employed it should be done in a way that is tested and experienced by the instructor to understand how the movement is affected and it needs to be properly documented on the client’s chart.
Gluteus Medius (Glutes/Hips) - Hip horizontal Abduction
Synergists:
Gluteus Minimus (Glutes/Hips) - Hip horizontal Abduction
Gluteus Maximus - lateral fibers (Glutes/Hips) - Hip horizontal Abduction
Piriformis - Hip horizontal Abduction
Considerations for setup:

The ABduction machine has a relatively simple set up. Similar to the ADduction machine, the seat back will most likely be standardized at position 6 or 7. This setting will allow for a more upright position when seated and is generally viewed as more favorable for our clients.

The main factor to be determined is the setting of the width of the thigh pads, which establishes the starting point and lower turnaround on this exercise, effectively the same as setting a gap. But there will likely never be a need for a gap on this machine because of the thigh pad adjustment.

Ideally we will look to have the thigh pads as “snug” or close together at the lower turnaround. We may even “crowd” or compress the subject's soft tissue to some extent to create as full an effective range of motion as possible.

As always, we should be attentive to the client’s level of comfort with any of the settings and if they are compressed too much or have had a history of hip issues, a slightly wider setting may be warranted.
Accordingly, we would expect subjects with larger lower bodies (wider hips/legs) to have a wider pad setting and smaller lower bodies will most likely have narrower settings.

The movement arms will need to be manually opened or pulled apart while the client enters the seat and lifts their legs for loading into the start position. If the weight is excessive and the movement arms cannot be pulled apart by the instructor, the weight can be set after the client is loaded into the machine. Just be prepared to assist the movement arms together (fully close them) with the leg so that the weight stack flattens fully and the selector pin can be placed into the weight stack. Take care in this approach as the client will most likely have their legs compressed to some degree.
Posture/Get Set:
Chest up, butt back, seat belt around waist (not on femurs), chin slightly tucked (neutral), feet and ankles relaxed, hands on handles for balance but not anchoring down.
Ideally this exercise will be performed with an anterior pelvic tilt, which is facilitated by the chest up, back arched posture.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:
LOAD UP:  From the starting position (lower turn), chest up, neutral head position, hands on handles, establish breathing, and gradually begin to apply pressure by driving out through the knees.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “good” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

CONCENTRIC/UPPER TURN:  Subject will move through this first concentric phase, lifting their chest, arching their back, and driving their knees apart “as far as they comfortably can” (upper turn). Once the desired duration is achieved in the contracted position (either brief pause of 1 second or slightly longer squeeze of 2 to 3 seconds), the instructor will click at that exact moment.
ECCENTRIC:  The click is immediately followed with the instruction to “ease out,  do not speed up” or something to that effect.

The instructor then needs to establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround of the set, which on an Abduction will be to “touch and go” or “be continuous” or “seamlessly change directions”. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.
LOWER TURN:  Touch and go at the lower turn as if “seamlessly changing directions without pausing.”
Keep chest up by leveraging off of the handles and the top of the back pad.

One continuous pace with only a “brief but definite” pause of about one second in the contracted position of the first two reps and a squeeze of two to three seconds from the third rep on. Keep in mind, we cannot simply rely on the cue of ‘squeeze’ in this situation. That can mean various things to different people. We need to teach them HOW to squeeze.

Verbiage for the pause/squeeze in the contracted position might be “lift your chest, arch your back, continue to drive out through your knees as if the movement continues…keep breathing, keep still, [click], ease out, don’t speed up” or “keeping your head still, drive your knees apart as hard as you can…there, lock it in place…breathe freely…[click], ease out.”  So during the desired duration of the squeeze in the contracted position, we are providing actionable instruction.

Importantly, the number of reps recorded will only be those that the instructor deems were full reps. So if the client does not reach full contraction of the upper back, that is not a full rep and will not be recorded in the rep count on the chart. But due to the nature of certain exercises, and Abduction being one of them, it may make sense to continue the set despite the client no longer achieving full range of motion. There will still be stimulative tension experienced on the partial reps as long as they are within the client’s exacting control.

The decision to continue a set after reaching concentric failure is highly individual and should be discussed with a studio Leader or with MSF Corporate. For a brand new client, just completing a handful of full range of motion reps may be enough to introduce the exercise. So in other words, we may not even take them to concentric failure if they are new to strength training or if they are showing signs of adverse discomfort or losing proper form. This is a progressive journey.

While we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.
NOTES

Be attentive to any pinch points while loading/unloading clients on this machine. Carefully pull the movement arms apart by grabbing the very end of the padding and slowly return them as the client lifts their legs. Additionally, watch for the thigh pads themselves as they tilt/rock in place and ensure the client’s hands are clear of them.

As with many exercises, we can expect each client to have varying capabilities in terms of range of motion. We should encourage as much of a ROM through hip abduction as is permitted. Additionally, the instructor should use the first 2 or 3 reps to determine what each individual subject’s ROM is and use that to determine encouragement of effort and registering full repetitions. In cases where ROM appears to be minimal, ensure that it does not result from excessive weight or a lack of understanding how to execute the movement.

While we are encouraging driving out through the knees, the knees may not in fact be in contact with the thigh pads. This is acceptable though in that to instruct driving out through the femur may be confusing and may not be as simply understood as through the singular point of the knee. The knee is essentially the end of the femur, which is the lever we are moving with our hip musculature on this exercise.

The instructor would then lead the client through an increasing STATIC effort against out into the thigh pads. This approach when followed at least weekly for months at a time can build an appreciable level of strength contributing to improved function of the hips. Importantly, while learning the Continuous Tension protocol, the subject will most likely be using a relatively light weight and as a result will probably be capable of performing a higher number of reps, spending more time on the machine. While this may seem conducive to learning, it can also be counterproductive from a discomfort standpoint. Yes, a big part of the learning curve is to be able to produce an effort while managing discomfort, but there can be diminishing returns in that the movement becomes intolerable before it is stimulative. To set the gap the instructor will clear the main weight stack (and accessory stack if not required) and establish control of the movement arms with their leg and hands. Keep hold of the main stack selector pin.
Ensure the movement arms are far enough apart and then have the client take a seat.

Begin to bring the movement arms together and instruct the client to lift their left leg up and into the left movement arm as you continue to slowly bring them together. Then when the movement arms are close enough, have the client lift their right leg into place, pushing the movement arms closer together to further assist if necessary. There is a timing and finesse to this process and the instructor should take a proactive approach in accommodating the client.
Once seated with legs in place, the instructor will carefully allow the movement arms to drift apart keeping their leg/hand against the mechanism to prevent sudden or excessive movement.

Once the gentle stretch has been reached, the instructor should place the selector pin into the desired weight and note the gap. Biceps Brachii (Biceps) - Elbow Flexion
Synergists:
Wrist Flexors - (Forearms) - Wrist stabilizer
Considerations for setup:

The primary consideration for this exercise will be the seat height. In most cases there will be a gap required depending on the location of the movement arm at rest relative to the client’s proportions and tolerance at the lower turnaround.
A standard gap of one or two will likely be required for the introduction of this exercise until the instructor can assess strength and tolerance at elbow extension.

While our Continuous Tension protocol has been developed with safety as the primary goal, there are certain exercises that carry more potential risk than others and the biceps curl is one of them. In particular it is the loading of the elbow joint in the stretched or extended position. For this reason we will use a gap at least when introducing this exercise.
Determine the seat height by first taking into account the height of the subject. Taller subjects will most likely have a lower seat, shorter subjects will have a higher seat.

Similar to the Triceps Extension, as a rotary movement, the Biceps Curl has a single axis of rotation and in theory, this axis is to be aligned with the axis of rotation of the body, the elbow joint. But because of differences in individual humerus lengths, there will be instances where direct alignment is not possible. As long as we can get close, there should be no negative impact on the safety or effectiveness of the exercise.

And just like the Triceps Extension, the proper seat height will allow the upper arm of the subject to lay flush along the pad. The subject should be sitting upright with their chest against the pad and their arms will lay over the pad  out in front of them. Ideally, the elbow crease will point more toward the ceiling than in towards each other. This requires a slight external rotation of the humeri.

If the seat were set too high, the upper arm would hover above the pad and the elbow would be the only point of the arm that made contact with the pad. Remember, the entire length of the upper arm (humerus) should lay along and make contact with the pad. If the seat were set too low, the elbow would not be able to make contact with the pad and the upper arm would rest at the peak of the bend in the pad. If the client mentions an uncomfortable pressure in the back of the arm (triceps) while performing the exercise, there is a good chance the seat is set too low.
Posture/Get Set:

This exercise utilizes a chest up posture while leaning into the chest pad. The arms will be outstretched over the top of the pad with the crease of the elbows pointing toward the ceiling. With the arms in this position, the instructor will lift the handle up from the resting position to remove any slack created by the belt and the kevlar belt. This will be the starting point and the lower turnaround.

The subject should reach for the handle and grab each side, palms up, equidistant from the center. One should always consider the required posture and the details of the load up as an integral component of the exercise itself.
To begin the movement, the instructor will maintain the starting position of the movement arm with an open hand and remind the client that “the exercise will begin from this position”.
Feet should be flat on the floor or alternatively if the subject has shorter legs with a higher seat, they can rest their feet back on the floor on the toes of the shoes.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

LOAD UP:  From the starting position (lower turn), chest up, neutral head position, face relaxed…establish breathing and gradually begin to apply pressure by driving the elbows down into the pad while simultaneously pulling up against the handles with just enough effort to begin moving. Keep in mind when a client properly performs a gradual load up, they will need to slightly speed up to stay smooth.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “mmm…hmm…” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

CONCENTRIC/UPPER TURN:  Subject will move through this first concentric phase maintaining a smooth pace, keeping their posture, and attempting to flex/close the elbow joints as tightly as they can (upper turn). It is important to note that most subjects will assume they are to pull the handles up as far as they possibly can. Not only will this lead to an unloading of the targeted muscles, but there will be an increased risk of bringing the movement arm up close to the face. The instructor must be certain to communicate the difference between loading and contracting the muscle and simply just moving the machine through space.

One continuous pace with only a “brief but definite” pause of about one second in the contracted position of the first two reps and a squeeze of two to three seconds from the third rep on. Keep in mind, we cannot simply rely on the cue of ‘squeeze’ in this situation. That can mean various things to different people. We need to teach them HOW to squeeze.

Verbiage for the pause/squeeze in the contracted position might be “continue to tighten your elbow joint as hard as you can…keep breathing, keep still, [click], ease out, don’t speed up” or “keeping your head still, clamp your elbow joints tight…there, lock it in place, [click], ease out.”  So during the desired duration of the squeeze in the contracted position, we are providing actionable instruction.
ECCENTRIC:  The click is immediately followed with the instruction to “ease out,  do not speed up” or something to that effect.

The instructor then needs to establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround of the set, which on the Biceps Curl will be to “touch and go” or “be continuous” or “seamlessly change directions”. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.
LOWER TURN:  Touch and go at the lower turn as if “continuously passing through the bottom.”

The instructor needs to stay attentive at this change of direction to make sure it is entirely within the client’s control. As mentioned above, there is an element of risk in this position that makes the elbow somewhat vulnerable under load. This will be mitigated with use of a gap as well as repeated practice and strengthening on this exercise.
Keep the chest up and the elbows firmly leveraged into the pad.

INTENSITY: By definition, the set will end when concentric failure is reached (i.e. subject can no longer reach the initially attained degree of elbow flexion with perfect form). This is where we would note the reps and record only the full reps achieved on the chart. But as discussed throughout the Academy, certain exercises lend themselves to performing additional, partial repetitions. So even though the subject cannot fully flex the elbow, there may be a substantial amount of strength remaining. Especially when they are able to perform those partial reps beyond the midpoint and with perfect form.

Of even more importance for the consideration of training beyond concentric failure (i.e. using partial repetitions) would be the experience and tolerance level of the individual. A newer, more deconditioned client would not yet be ready for this more advanced technique. They can simply perform full repetitions to a point where they begin to fatigue and the effort will probably be enough to provide the desired stimulus. Of course we are always attempting to progress every client’s understanding of effort and intensity while improving their quality from session to session as is illustrated in the point below.

While we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.
NOTES

The trainer will click only after they have visually confirmed that the desirable range of motion has been achieved and the movement has temporarily ceased (i.e. no further contraction of the biceps is possible). The instructor needs to be attentive to the likelihood that the client will assume that the movement should continue until they hear the click. But the opposite is true. The [click] will ONLY come when the proper range of motion has been achieved and the client has established control (brief pause in contracted position). So these two objectives are at odds and the instructor needs to anticipate and be assertive to control the outcome. This will be yet another example of how the trainer cares more about the workout than the client does.

There is typically a one or a two gap that will be used on this exercise, at least during the introduction. If certain subjects show a level of strength and control, we may reduce the gap or eliminate it altogether. Keep in mind that a longer range of motion and a deeper stretch are not necessarily better. This will be highly individual and should be taken on a case by case basis. But there is some benefit to loading certain muscles while they are being lengthened. As long as the stretch is not excessive, and there is still some degree of elbow bend at the lower turnaround, certain subjects will be able to utilize the full range of motion.

This exercise may be performed isometrically for individuals with an injury such as tennis or golfers elbow. (Static Hold or Timed Static Contraction). As with all static holds, the instructor will assist the subject to the position in which the exercise will be performed and will take the movement arm back to the resting position when finished. See the section on Static Holds and Timed Static Contractions for more details on the setup and execution.

Importantly, while learning the Continuous Tension protocol, the subject will most likely be using a relatively light weight and as a result will probably be capable of performing a higher number of reps, spending more time on the machine. While this may seem conducive to learning, it can also be counterproductive from a discomfort standpoint. Yes a big part of the learning curve is to be able to produce an effort while managing discomfort, but there can be diminishing returns in that the movement becomes intolerable before it is stimulative. Ideally we should be striving for perfect form with “faster” reps (i.e. 6 second positive, 6 second negative) and a “heavier” weight that leads to failure in 10 or fewer reps. While this may not be achievable or advisable in the initial sessions, as long as the subject is demonstrating a clear understanding of the control required, we may progress the intensity more quickly.

Among the biggest discrepancies to be expected on this machine will be to lift the upper arms and elbows off the pad, even subtly, to be able to pull the movement arm up further. In conjunction with this, there will be a tendency to curl or flex the wrists to move the handles further. But this again falls under the assumed objective of exercise, which is to keep the movement arm moving or to move it further. The instructor must continually watch for these tendencies and remind the client of the real objective; to create as much tension in the targeted muscle fibers as possible at that moment. By lifting the arms off the pad, we unload the biceps and outsource the effort to other muscles. This concept will most likely be the most challenging one to convince clients of and the most important.

Considerations for setup:
There are several considerations when establishing the settings for a client on the Cervical Extension, along with the need to satisfy the Theoretical versus Practical alignment.

The most sensible place to start will be the seat height. Determine the seat height by first taking into account the height of the subject. Taller subjects will most likely have a lower seat, shorter subjects will have a higher seat.

As a rotary movement, the Cervical Extension has a single axis of rotation and in theory, this axis is to be aligned with the axis of rotation of the body, near the middle of the neck. This will most likely be somewhere around C3 to C5.

This will approximate the alignment of the axis of rotation on the vertical plane. There must also be an alignment horizontally and this will be accomplished by having the subject sit more forward or more rearward on the seat. The instructor must pull the movement arm (head pad) back to create the space for the subject to sit down. Most subjects will likely be sitting somewhere in the middle of the seat. If they were to sit all the way back on the seat, which will probably be their instinctive assumption, they will most likely be positioned entirely behind the axis.

After determining the seat height and position on the seat, the theoretical alignment will be established. At this point the seat back can be brought forward to make light contact with the subject’s mid back. Note, the back pad should NOT push the subject more forward and thus out of alignment.

The next consideration is the most important and is what is referred to as the practical alignment. Having already aligned the subject with the axis from the theoretical standpoint, there needs to be an assurance that those settings allow for the movement arm (head pad) to fit securely on the back of the head. This will ultimately govern the final settings on the Cervical Extension.

Again, the instructor will manually control the movement arm and pull the head pad back to allow the subject to sit. Having the subject sit as upright as possible and placing the hands on the handles in front of them, carefully bring the movement arm forward so that the head pad meets the back of the head.

It is critical to get this alignment correct. The back of the head needs to perfectly seat into the opening of the head pad. The most secure and most comfortable placement will likely have the most protruding portion of the back of the head in the open recess of the head pad.

If the seat is too low, the back of the head will be at the bottom of the head pad and the head pad will likely begin to slide up and over the top of the head (or it will feel as though the pad will slide up on the subject’s head).
If the seat is too high, the back of the head will be above the opening on the head pad.

Even if there appears to be a perfect alignment while seated in the neutral position at the point of the movement arm transfer, once the subject begins to perform the exercise, there may be some sliding or movement of the head on the pad. This should not happen. In this case, it may make sense to have the subject either move slightly forward or slightly rearward on the seat. This will only be done while NOT under load. Any adjustment to position should be directed by the instructor and the movement arm should be entirely under the instructor’s control.
There will be no gap on this machine as the lower turnaround will either be the full excursion of the movement arm or as much of a stretch (flexion) as feels comfortable to the subject.

Most clients will start with 20 pounds, the lightest increment available on this exercise. In the event that a client is injured or severely deconditioned, it may be advised to perform this exercise in a static fashion. See Notes section below for more detail.
Posture/Get Set:

The Cervical Extension requires an interpersonal transfer of weight (i.e. handoff) and the instructor must become skilled enough through practice to perform this properly. In order for the client to sit, the movement arm must be pulled back and controlled by the instructor.
Chest up, feet flat on floor (or platform or heels on platform depending on height and leg length), hands on handles with elbows in, chin slightly elevated to receive movement arm.

Client must be sitting upright with an exaggerated posture. Maintaining a proper, extended lower back throughout the exercise is critical. Although some thoracic movement may be necessary during the dynamic execution. See more in the Execution section below.

With the movement arm secured by the instructor, clear direction needs to be given to get the client properly positioned and aligned with the movement arm. The client should be holding a firm, upright position as the instructor brings the movement arm closer to the back of the client’s head.

The instructor will then allow the head pads to make contact with the back of the head while cueing any necessary adjustments to better align the client. Usually commands such as, “sit taller…chin up/down…scoot forward” will be effective in ensuring a secure seating of the head to the head pads. Client will be in a relatively neutral head position as this will be the safest and strongest point to receive the load. Importantly, the instructor should stand to the side of the client to better assess this alignment.

The trainer will then gradually begin to transfer the weight to the client while giving the verbal indicator “that is yours,” or something to that effect. The client needs to hold the movement arm still to establish control before beginning the eccentric. If there is movement during the handoff the trainer should not yet fully transfer the load. Instruct the client to “increase your force” or “push harder” or “don’t move”.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

After a proper handoff, the instructor will cue the client to “slowly begin to allow the head to come forward…trying to maintain consistent contact with the head pad”. The first movement is the eccentric phase into neck flexion. Remember there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of every exercise.

This next suggestion is critical to the movement. In some cases, in order to maintain a consistent, flush contact point with the back of the head against the head pad, the torso will have to move. More specifically, the ribcage may need to drop slightly as the head moves forward and then rise as the head moves back into cervical extension. The degree of movement of the ribcage will be entirely dictated by the requirement to maintain flush contact with the head pad. While this may not be ideal in theory, it may be necessary to keep the movement smooth and continuous, ultimately making it safer.

While still in the first eccentric, and possibly allowing the ribcage to drop to accommodate the contact with the head pad, the instructor will cue the client to “allow the head to come forward as far as [you] feel comfortable. In the event that [you] are able to allow the weights to touch, do so with a continuous/seamless change of direction.”
Another helpful cue to maintain a smooth execution is to “always attempt to push squarely into the head pad” or “keep your head in the path of the machine, don’t try and create your own path.”

Once they have changed direction, the instructor will want to remind the client to “keep lifting your head/chin while you lift your chest and arch your back.”  The client will most likely not know how far back to go so something like “follow it all the way, back and down” or “head to butt, butt to head” can be helpful in encouraging the full extension pattern we are seeking with this movement.

The upper turnaround (and squeeze) will occur when the subject has extended their cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine to the fullest extent possible. This will vary between individuals and the instructor should note the exact range of motion for every client.

The trainer will click only after they have visually confirmed that the desirable range of motion has been achieved and the movement has temporarily ceased (i.e. no further contraction of the extensors is possible). The instructor needs to be attentive to the likelihood that the client will assume that the movement should continue until they hear the click. But the opposite is true. The click will ONLY come when the proper range of motion has been achieved and the client has established full control with a brief pause in contracted position.
Verbiage used on the concentric might be to “try and draw a rainbow/arch with the top of your head from front to back.”

But of paramount importance is the fact that the Cervical Extension should NEVER be taken to failure. There is a greater likelihood that the subject will change their behavior/execution as a result of the increasing perceived exertion. Stay within the tolerable limit of each individual client, making sure that every rep is able to be completed with exacting control. Always take a conservative approach and perform fewer reps than they appear capable of. In other words, stop the set early especially during the first few times on the machine. Over time we will get a better understanding of their capability and the client will become stronger and use better control. Then and only then can we begin to progress to a more intense approach. But again, NEVER take the set to failure.
NOTES

While we at MSF have gone out of our way to ensure that the client’s safety remains our number one priority, we still must acknowledge that certain exercises pose more of a potential risk than others. Cervical Extension would most likely be one of those exercises. There is more risk for the obvious reason that the cervical spine is having to control an external load. Even if someone has never strength trained before, they will likely experience many physical endeavors throughout the course of a normal day as they carry groceries or walk up stairs or perform yard work. While the neck muscles are required to work all day long as they are tasked with holding up our heads, an additional, external load is an uncommon situation.

A common discrepancy on this exercise usually involves the subject not understanding the path that the head and neck must travel through to perform this movement correctly. They will often push or resist against the head pad in a linear path. But being that this movement is a single joint exercise and therefore rotary in nature, the instructor must teach and remind the client that the head should move about the axis of the neck beneath it. As mentioned above, the image of drawing an arch or a rainbow with the top of the head from front to back can be helpful. Or to remind the client that they will be constantly either lifting or lowering their nose/chin as they execute the movement. Another common discrepancy is for the client to simply rotate up and down in place, causing the head to slide against the head pad. So there is zero travel of the movement arm in this case even though they are moving their head. Again, they must be reminded to bring their entire head forward and down, tucking the chin, on the eccentric, and then pushing back and down, lifting their chin and arching their back on the concentric.

This exercise may also be performed isometrically for safety or education purposes (Static Hold or Timed Static Contraction). Just like any static hold, the instructor will load the client and take the weight away at the end. There is no movement with a static exercise. On the cervical extension specifically, the best position to perform the static tends to be just beyond neutral. So biased toward the concentric where the subject will have their chin slightly elevated. They must be reminded to push back AND down to maintain that position. Remember that while there is no movement on a static, they must still direct their effort in a direction. As discussed above, the natural inclination is to want to push straight back, when in fact it should be simultaneously back and down.

It should go without saying that due to the awkward nature of the movement and the unfamiliarity of an external load against the head, that the cervical extension should NEVER be taken to failure and should be progressed slowly. A conservative approach should be taken with the number of reps performed too, even with what is deemed a lighter weight. Anything over 8 reps might be considered excessive unless it was a seasoned trainee with a lot of experience on this exercise.

As with any interpersonal transfer (hand off) of a movement arm, it needs to be rehearsed and perfected by the instructor. The instructor needs to control the entire process with clear, concise cueing and manage the movement arm entirely until there is one hundred percent certainty that the subject has control of the load and is properly positioned.

Considerations for setup:
There are several considerations when establishing the settings for a client on the Chest Flye, along with the need to satisfy Theoretical versus Practical alignment.
Determine the seat height by first taking into account the height of the subject. Taller subjects will most likely have a lower seat, shorter subjects will have a higher seat.

The seat will need to be fine tuned so that the upper arm (humerus) is sloped down slightly from the shoulder to the elbow, or at least level to the floor, when in the starting position. So the humeral head in the shoulder joint would be slightly higher than the elbow, or level, when the hands are on the handles.
Additionally, the top of the head will end up near the padded “work box” overhead when seated.

The theoretical alignment in this case would have the subject’s shoulders directly under the axes of rotation of the machine, which is determined by the back pad. However, what tends to be more important is the resulting location of the elbows/humerus on the roller pads and the need for a sufficient amount of space between the roller pads and the subject in the contracted position. This is the practical alignment that will govern the most optimal settings.

Accordingly, we would expect subjects with longer arms to have the back pad set further back, away from the roller pads. And subjects with shorter arms would have the back pad set in closer to the roller pads. But the following point must also be taken into consideration.

As a result of the need to satisfy the practical alignment, look to position the back pad so that when sitting upright with arms out to the sides and hands on the handles, the elbow will land beyond the roller pad. And more importantly, the elbow will remain in a position beyond the roller pad throughout the full ROM. If the back pad is too far back, the elbow (i.e. humerus) may not stay in contact with roller pads during the movement. Alternatively, if the back pad is too far forward, the roller pads may run into the client as they perform the movement.
Importantly, given the juxtaposed situations outlined in the two points above, we need to consider the interplay of arm length AND torso size to find the optimal back pad setting.

Once the seat and chest pad are set, we will need to consider a gap to create a more conservative stretch at the starting point/lower turnaround. Most subjects will benefit by starting the movement with the elbow slightly behind the midline of the torso when viewed from the side (frontal plane). This will provide a slight stretch for most. A subject with shoulder issues will warrant a more conservative approach and should most likely have a larger gap, resulting in a reduced stretch. As always, tolerance should be assessed on an individual basis.

Chest up, butt back, feet on stool, chin slightly tucked (neutral), arms behind the roller pads with hands on handles.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

LOAD UP:  From the starting position (lower turn), keeping chest up, neutral head position, arms in place, establish breathing, and gradually begin to apply pressure by driving forward through the elbows.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “mmm, hmm” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

CONCENTRIC/UPPER TURN:  Subject will move through this first concentric phase, maintaining a chest up posture and driving the elbows together until the roller pads make contact (upper turn). Once the desired duration is achieved in the contracted position (either brief pause of 1 second or slightly longer squeeze of 2 to 3 seconds), the instructor will “click” to begin the eccentric.
ECCENTRIC:  The click is immediately followed with the instruction to “ease out, keep that pace” or something to that effect.

LOWER TURN: Now that the client is in the first eccentric phase of the set, the instructor must inform the client of what will constitute the lower turnaround and what the client is expected to do there. In this case the client will “touch and go” or “be continuous at the bottom” or “barely touch, barely start” or “seamlessly change direction as the weights touch” or “soft touch, do not pause.”  All of those cues require the client to control their pace and increase their focus as they sense for the exact moment the weights touch. Again, this creates a level of safety we require with our Continuous Tension protocol. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.

One continuous pace with only a “brief but definite” pause of about one second in the contracted position of the first two reps and a squeeze of two to three seconds from the third rep on. Keep in mind, we cannot simply rely on the cue of ‘squeeze’ in this situation. That can mean various things to different people. We need to teach them HOW to squeeze.

Verbiage for the pause/squeeze in the contracted position for the Chest Flye might be “keep your chest up and gently bring those pads together…now keep breathing and continue to drive through your elbows, attempting to further dent those pads…keep still…[click], ease out…don’t speed up.”  So during the desired duration of the squeeze, we are providing actionable instruction.
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and contact with the arm pads.

Importantly, the number of reps recorded will only be those that the instructor deems were full reps. So if the client does not reach full contraction of the chest, that is not a full rep and will not be recorded in the rep count on the chart. But due to the nature of certain exercises, and Chest Flye being one of them, it may make sense to continue the set despite the client no longer achieving full range of motion (see point below). There will still be stimulative tension experienced on the partial reps as long as they are within the client’s exacting control.

The decision to continue a set after reaching concentric failure is highly individual and should be discussed with a studio Leader or with MSF Corporate. For a brand new client, just completing a handful of full range of motion reps may be enough to introduce the exercise. This is a progressive journey.

Subject will place the heel of the palm on the bend of the handle. This will create a semi-pronated grip with the thumb side of the hands slightly rotated upward (begin to supinate from a palms down position).

Ensure the weight stack is clear and assist the handles out to the end stop. Ideally the subject will be able to just fully straighten at the elbow without protracting or rounding forward. Ensure the movement arm mechanism will clear the top of the head of the subject. If not, or if it is close it may be advisable to move the chest pad further back, which will likely require a larger gap of the weight stack.

The default setting for the width of the handles is the middle position (noted on the chart with an ‘M’). If someone had a smaller frame or we were seeking to bias the lats we might use the narrow setting (‘N’ on the chart). And if our goal was to bias more of the upper back, or the client had a larger/wider build, we might use the wide setting and note that on the chart with ‘W’. In any case, we need to be consistent with the handle setting in that particular workout of the rotation. Each handle will have its own settings that correspond to the resulting limb length and will have its own targeted musculature. Random variation or lack of consistency may negatively impact the workout at worst or at the very least create a misleading metric on the chart.
Posture/Get Set:

Chest up, hips back, chin slightly tucked (neutral) with slight lean forward into the chest pad. If the subject sits too close to the chest pad and the hips are either against or tucked under the chest pad, there will be a temptation to lean away from the chest pad. This can increase the contribution from the low back which is not desirable on this movement.

The client and the trainer will pull the handles back together to a position just beyond the midpoint but not to the fully contracted position. The client will not likely be able to hold this position when handed off.
The loads tend to be heavier on this exercise and the leverage is poor for the assisting instructor, so the client has to be able to reach the handles and contribute.

It is also advisable for the instructor to establish a wide base with their stance so they can better leverage their bodyweight in the assist rather than just the arms. Additionally, since the client will most likely be using the neutral handles, the instructor should grab the bottom of the movement arm with one hand and the pronated handle with the other hand.

The trainer will then gradually transfer the weight to the client (i.e. handoff) while giving the verbal indicator “that is yours,” or something to that effect. The client needs to hold the movement arm still to establish control before beginning the eccentric. If there is movement during the handoff the trainer should not yet fully transfer the load. Instruct the client to “increase your force” or “pull harder.”
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

The movement requires an instructor assist as the set will start near the contracted position (upper turn). The scapular retraction component of the row is paramount to the movement pattern so the transfer and brief hold while contracting will remind them of the feeling we are seeking. After an accurate handoff, the instructor will cue the client to “slowly begin to let the arms straighten,” or to “begin lowering the movement arm.”  Remember there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.

Once the subject’s arms straighten, they will “continuously” or “seamlessly” or “immediately” begin bending them again. (Importantly, ‘immediate’ means right away, but does not mean suddenly in this case). This is the lower turnaround on a compound row and in most cases the weights will NOT touch here. But it may also help to have the weights touch just as the arms straighten for clients who may be inconsistent with their range of motion or to protect a valgus elbow.

The upper turnaround (squeeze) will be when the subject has fully contracted their upper back where the elbows travel beyond the torso or the upper arm aligns with the side of the torso in the event of a more lat biased row.

Most subjects will assume that they should pull the handles back as far as they can, lifting the weights higher. The instructor should remind them of the real objective to focus on the optimal range of motion for the muscles being targeted.

The trainer will click only after they have visually confirmed that the desirable range of motion has been achieved and the movement has temporarily ceased (i.e. no further contraction is possible). The instructor needs to be attentive to the likelihood that the client will assume that the movement should continue until they hear the click. But the opposite is true. The click will ONLY come when the proper range of motion has been achieved and the client has established control (brief pause in a chest up scapular retraction). So these two objectives are at odds and the instructor needs to anticipate and be assertive to control the outcome. This will be yet another example of how the trainer cares more about the workout than the client does.

Verbiage used on the concentric might be to “draw the shoulders back (or together) as hard as possible” or to “pull with the shoulder blades.”  For a lat biased row, the instruction might be to “keep your chest up and pull the elbows into the sides of the torso.”

Maintain posture, head position, pace, and arm path. Elbows should track through the same path concentrically and eccentrically, whether wide or narrow to ensure consistent loading of target musculature.

INTENSITY: By definition, the set will end when concentric failure is reached (i.e. subject can no longer lift the weight with perfect form). This is where we would note the reps and record only the full reps achieved on the chart. But as discussed throughout the Academy, certain exercises lend themselves to performing additional, partial repetitions and the Compound Row is one of these movements. Especially when the client is able to perform those partial reps beyond the midpoint and with perfect form. Of even more importance for the consideration of training beyond concentric failure (i.e. using partial repetitions) would be the experience and tolerance level of the individual. A newer, more deconditioned client would not yet be ready for this more advanced technique. They can simply perform full repetitions to a point where they begin to fatigue and the effort will probably be enough to provide the desired stimulus. Of course we are always attempting to progress every client’s understanding of effort and intensity while improving their quality from session to session as is illustrated in the point below.

While we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.
NOTES
Ensure that the mechanism at the top of the movement arms is far enough away from the top of the clients’ head while entering, exiting, and training.
The neutral handle option will likely be the most shoulder friendly position and will target a more overall area including both lats and upper back. As a result this is our default hand position.

The handles should just be within fingertip reach while unloaded so that the client can assist the trainer (and vice versa) into the contracted position during the load up. And then the client can set the weight down without assistance to unload at the end of the set.

In general, a narrower arm path (elbows in) will result in a more lat biased movement while an abducted arm path (elbows out) will bias the upper back musculature. Keep in mind that the more we seek to target the upper back muscles (rhomboids, traps) the more scapular protraction and retraction we should encourage.

There will be some clients that have a valgus elbow characterized by an abnormal outward angle of the forearm relative to the humerus. In more severe cases, movement at the elbow (often on the eccentric) will result in varying degrees of discomfort. A shortened range of motion that limits elbow extension may be beneficial or performing a pushing movement first can help. If either of those strategies do not alleviate the issue, it may be beneficial to try the pronated handles.

Keep in mind with a pronated grip, the upper arm path will need to be wider and the elbows should travel well past the midline of torso in the contracted position. This may be used to emphasize the upper back muscles and will create another variation on the row that can be added for a more advanced client.

Height of the chest pad will most likely be dictated by the height, or length of spine, of the client. Some exceptions may include raising the chest pad to the uppermost position to account for a larger abdomen, or lowering the chest pad if the client is experiencing discomfort from the pressure against the sternum.

Importantly, while learning the Continuous Tension protocol, the subject will most likely be using a relatively light weight and as a result will probably be capable of performing a higher number of reps, spending more time on the machine. While this may seem conducive to learning, it can also be counterproductive from a discomfort standpoint. Yes a big part of the learning curve is to be able to produce an effort while managing discomfort, but there can be diminishing returns in that the movement becomes intolerable before it is stimulative. Ideally we should be striving for perfect form with “faster” reps (i.e. 6 second positive, 6 second negative) and a “heavier” weight that leads to failure in 10 or fewer reps. While this may not be achievable or advisable in the initial sessions, as long as the subject is demonstrating a clear understanding of the control required, we may progress the intensity more quickly.

Considerations for setup:

LC will most likely have a gap of 2 or 3 as an introduction to this exercise (this will be determined by the Studio Leader and MSF Corp). A gap of 3 or more may be advised for those with knee injuries/issues.
Move the seat back to the rearmost position leaving the largest possible area on the seat.

Have the subject sit with their femurs cantilevered off the front of the seat and the lower leg hanging. They may need to raise at least one of their knees to approximate the roller pad (also referred to as the shin or tibia pad). The knee should align with the axis of rotation of the machine, which puts the knee cap at the edge of the roller pad but NOT under the pad. No part of the patella can be under the roller pad as this is extremely uncomfortable and puts the knee in a position of hyperextension. Instead the patellas should “crowd” the roller pad with the top of the tibia under the pad.

Have the subject remain seated but lean forward slightly (they may need to hold on to the frame for balance, it is safe to do at this point because we will not yet be moving the weight stack). Then carefully bring the back pad forward to just make contact with the subject’s lower back (note: the seat back should not push them further forward as the knees will then go forward of the axis of rotation). Have the subject sit all the way back in the seat and verify that the knees are still in alignment with the axis of rotation.
Once the seat setting is determined, have the subject exit and stand so that the weight can be selected and they may be properly loaded into the machine.

Due to the unfamiliarity a new client will have with the pressure of the force couple from the movement arm acting on the knee joint in the starting position of the LC, there will most likely be a standard gap of at least 1 and maybe 2. This will depend on the size of the client’s lower body and the mobility they possess at the knee joint. Larger legs and hip girdles will require more room and a larger gap at the starting point to avoid potential hyperextension at the knee. This standardized gap may vary slightly between machines and should be discussed with the MSF Corporate team during installation.

Set the appropriate weight, again with a gap of 1 or 2 or as otherwise determined for that particular client on that particular LC machine. Then, using the assist bar attached to the movement arm, pull the movement arm down to an approximate midpoint. Facing the client in the trainer will want to shift over to the left and use their right knee on the calf pad to assist in pulling the movement arm down. This will also leave room for the client to sit on the corner of the seat and sweep their legs in from the side and between the roller pads. Carefully lower the weight to set the movement arm into the starting position (client’s legs will now be extended out in front of them). Assess the location of the knee joint relative to the axis of rotation and the proximity of the patella to the roller pad.

ALTERNATIVE LOADING METHOD: In the event that the weight being used is too heavy to be moved with the assist bar and knee, just set the desired weight only on the accessory stack and move the tibia pad out of the way. With this technique, the trainer will only be lifting the 20 pounds on the main stack and whatever weight is needed for the working set on the accessory stack. The trainer will then lower the movement arm so that the weight stack reveals the desired gap. Note that because of the lack of weight acting on the movement arm the trainer may have to force the mechanism back against the passive tension of the subject’s legs. Then tactfully reach across the client’s body to select the proper main stack weight and gap.

Once seated and in place in the force couple of the movement arm, the instructor will need to consider adjusting the calf pad. This is the other roller pad of the two that belong to the movement arm. Ideally, the calf pad will make contact with the lowest part of the back of the leg, in a position that is just above the achilles tendon (i.e. above the heel). Keep in mind because this setting is on a circular path and not simply linear, it may create a tighter or looser fit. In most cases, a tighter fit that is still comfortable will be ideal. As such, the trainer may have to consider altering the gap in light of changing the calf pad setting.
Posture/Get Set:

Chest up - lay back against the angle of the seat with the head upright in a neutral position looking forward. Secure seat belt tightly across hip crease. Hands on handles pulling up for leverage. Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “perfect” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

Subject will move through this first concentric phase until the knees are maximally bent, with the “click” after the brief pause or squeeze (or wherever strength, effort, and individual range of motion permit movement).
After the load up and first concentric, and immediately after the click, the instructor may cue “ease out and do not speed up.”

The instructor then needs to establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround of the set, which on the leg curl will be to “touch and go” or “be continuous” or “barely touch, barely start”. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.
Touch and go at the lower turn as if “seamlessly passing through the change of direction.”
Keep hips down by anchoring with the hands.

After the lower turnaround at the beginning of the third rep, the client will dorsiflex their ankles. This should take place AFTER the change of direction and should be seamlessly activated during the concentric. Encourage the client to “keep the ankles relaxed during the turn…now pull the feet up to the knees [give visual demonstration if necessary].”

As the client approaches the upper turn (contracted position) we might give the cue to “keep the ankles flexed, keep the movement arm still, keep breathing, [click], relax the ankles, THEN ease out.”  Note that the ankles are relaxed while still in the contracted position. No movement occurs while client relaxes their ankles. Then they ease out of the contracted position. These are two separate actions that take place sequentially. Relax the ankles first, THEN begin to lower the weight.

One continuous pace with only a “brief but definite” pause of about one second in the contracted position of the first two reps and a squeeze of two to three seconds from the third rep on. Keep in mind, we cannot simply rely on the cue of ‘squeeze’ in this situation. That can mean various things to different people. We need to teach them HOW to squeeze.

Verbiage for the pause/squeeze in the contracted position might be “pulling up on the handles, drive your knees into the roller pad while pulling your heels toward your rear end, keep breathing, keep still, [click], relax your ankles, THEN ease out, don’t speed up” or “keeping your head still, bend your knees as tightly as you can, there, lock it in place, [click], ease out.”  So during the desired duration of the squeeze in the contracted position, we are providing useful direction.

Maintain posture, head position, pace, and contact on roller pads. The only movement on this exercise is at the knee joint and maybe the arms resulting from an increased need for leverage from the handles. Everything else is held still.

Importantly, the number of reps recorded will only be those that the instructor deems were full reps. So if the client does not reach full flexion of the knee (for them), that is not a full rep and will not be recorded in the rep count on the chart. But due to the nature of certain exercises, and leg curl being one of them, it may make sense to continue the set despite the client no longer achieving full range of motion. There will still be stimulative tension experienced on the partial reps as long as they are within the client’s exacting control.

For a brand new client, just completing a handful of full range of motion reps may be enough to introduce the exercise. So in other words, we may not even take them to concentric failure if they are new to strength training or if they are showing signs of adverse discomfort or losing proper form. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.
NOTES

It may be necessary or beneficial to describe “gradual” to the subject (e.g. 20 pounds of pressure, 40 pounds, 60 pounds, eventually reaching enough force to begin moving). Or have client imagine that there was 100 pounds on weight stack and they are to gradually find 101 pounds of pressure, or just enough to crack the weight stack. Also remind them that this gradual load up may take 3 to 5 seconds before movement actually occurs. We might give imagery of just barely beginning to dent the roller pads by bending the knees and increasing pressure from there.

We give the instruction to relax the feet and ankles on the first two reps and begin to flex the ankles during the concentric from the third rep on. The idea behind this is to just use the hamstrings on the first two reps while the subject is at full strength. Then after the first two reps, by flexing the ankles (dorsiflexion), we are gaining leverage for the calf (gastrocnemius) to contribute. It will increase strength on the concentric and allow for a tighter contraction (squeeze) at the upper turnaround. The ankles are then relaxed to allow only the hamstring to lower the weight as all muscles are stronger on the eccentric. Once practiced enough times, this “toggling” between flexing and relaxing the ankles feels natural and is a synergistic action in this movement pattern. While it may seem like an overthought detail, it is an effective way to establish control of the load, heighten awareness of the targeted muscles, and can increase motor unit recruitment.

As discussed above, it is imperative that the MSF Exercise Practitioner become keenly aware of how much intensity to provide each individual client on every exercise in each workout. As a general rule, the newer, more deconditioned a client is, the less intensity is required to create a stimulus (i.e. positive effect). So it will be in their best interest to introduce the concept of resistance training more conservatively. Start lighter and teach them how to control the movement. They’ll be better able to receive instruction when they’re not overwhelmed by the struggle. We still absolutely need to teach them intensity and progress their effort and quality but it will be a slower, longer process for these types. Again, show the client that we care more about their workout than they do!

The leg curl has a reputation for creating cramps or “fear of cramps” from its subjects. There will often be feedback during a set along the lines of “it feels like my legs are cramping” or “it feels like my muscles are tearing.”  While we should certainly entertain the discussion with genuine concern, it is more likely that these are just sensations resulting from the unfamiliar nature of knee flexion against a resistance. Most people will bend the knee in the course of everyday life but few will load the knee flexion pattern directly. To add to this, it seems that the modern day lifestyle has led to a tighter, possibly shorter hamstring. After enough sessions and as strength increases, this sensation will most likely go away completely.

We may find that the client is physically incapable of fully bending one or both knees. If this is the case, then we need to redefine what is a full range of motion for that client (this should be noted on the chart with “limited ROM” or “limit flexion” for purposes of consistency session to session and trainer to trainer).

As an added tool in the toolbox here, we may decide for those subjects that lack full knee flexion, to use a hard end stop at THEIR contracted position (upper turn). This is accomplished by using the extra selector pin and placing it in the main stack pin above the weight stack so that it makes contact with the top of the frame at the subject’s approximate upper turnaround (document the # of empty holes between the top of the weight stack and the location of the selector pin). Over time, we may be able to increase the range of motion (by lowering the pin) as the subject gets stronger.

It’s not as though the fully contracted position is the only beneficial part of the movement pattern and it may be argued that there is no additive benefit from a hypertrophy standpoint from that full contraction. It is useful however, not only in establishing a consistency in execution and range of motion, but in allowing the client to “feel” the working muscles. To assist in creating that mental connection, which can contribute to an increase in motor unit recruitment (MUR). Additionally, it is technically more difficult to lift the weight further and fully contract, which allows for a lighter more conservative weight to be used while still providing all of the challenge we seek.

It’s not as though the fully contracted position is the only beneficial part of the movement pattern and it may be argued that there is no additive benefit from a hypertrophy standpoint from that full contraction. It is useful however, not only in establishing a consistency in execution and range of motion, but in allowing the client to “feel” the working muscles. To assist in creating that mental connection which can contribute to an increase in motor unit recruitment (MUR). Additionally, it is technically more difficult to lift the weight further and fully contract, which allows for a lighter more conservative weight to be used while still providing all of the challenge we seek.

Many subjects will come to us with knee issues and may or may not be able to tolerate this movement pattern. While avoiding this exercise altogether would be the most conservative approach overall, we may be able to actually help the client by strengthening the area. For those with no underlying orthopedic issue, the most conservative approach would be to perform a Timed Static Contraction (TSC). In this situation, the instructor would pin a heavy enough weight so that the movement arm cannot be moved (i.e. too heavy to actually lift). Then, with the client properly secured in the seat, the instructor will position the movement arm to some approximate midpoint in the range of motion, maybe slightly biased toward the upper turnaround. The instructor would then lead the client through an increasing STATIC effort against the back pad. This is typically a 50% effort for 30 seconds, a 75% effort for another 30 seconds, and a final 30 seconds at an all out effort, for a total of 90 seconds of continuous effort. This approach when followed at least weekly for months at a time can build an appreciable level of strength contributing to improved function of the knees. There also tends to be a carryover effect to what has been estimated at 15 degrees in either direction of the position of the static exercise. There is also a possibility that the client will be able to one day perform this exercise dynamically and continue to progress.

Another option available that is more conservative than dynamic exercise but slightly less conservative than TSC is what we call a Static Hold (SH). A Static Hold, as the name implies is another variation of a static exercise protocol, so there is no movement. But it differentiates itself from a TSC in that during a SH the subject is actually holding weight, whereas in a TSC the subject is NOT holding weight but is producing their own force against an immovable movement arm. For the LE, the trainer can select a conservative but challenging load and set the selector pin in a hole above the weight stack so that when the movement arm is advanced, the selector pin will abut the top of the frame thus prohibiting further positive/concentric movement. But in order to keep this alternative method safe, the instructor must assist the client (and the movement arm) into the static hold position. This can be a significant challenge at heavier loads and may not be advisable if the instructor cannot lift the movement arm into place. The instructor must also assist the movement arm down into the resting position at the completion of the targeted time. SH’s are typically introduced at a time interval of 30 to 45 seconds maximum to assess tolerance. With continued use, the client can progress up to a time 120 seconds. After that, the duration can become excessive and may become more of an act of tolerance rather than a tool used to create tension. Once a client can sustain an effort for 120 seconds, it may be advisable to increase the load, decrease the time, and begin to progress 10 seconds or so at a time.

Importantly, while learning the Continuous Tension protocol, the subject will most likely be using a relatively light weight and as a result will probably be capable of performing a higher number of reps, spending more time on the machine. While this may seem conducive to learning, it can also be counterproductive from a discomfort standpoint. Yes a big part of the learning curve is to be able to produce an effort while managing discomfort, but there can be diminishing returns in that the movement becomes intolerable before it is stimulative. Ideally we should be striving for perfect form with “faster” reps (i.e. 6 second positive, 6 second negative) and a “heavier” weight that leads to failure in 10 or fewer reps. While this may not be achievable or advisable in the initial sessions, as long as the subject is demonstrating a clear understanding of the control required, we may progress the intensity more quickly.
