Considerations for setup:

Determine position of seat back. Default of position 2 (P2) will be optimal for most. Larger subjects may benefit from a position 3 as it will allow for less congestion around the midsection. Also in situations where subjects may not tolerate a certain amount of hip flexion, P3 may serve them well. Just keep in mind that the trade off for a more reclined position can be more pressure from the shoulder pads as well as a greater potential for the hips to rise out of the seat. Both of which are undesirable and should be monitored by the instructor.

Set shoulder pads so they are touching top of shoulders when subject is laying back in seat. At this point in the setup, it is recommended to have the full accessory stack pinned at 18 pounds to facilitate the next steps. The main stack should be clear with the instructor holding the selector pin, while 18 pounds is set on the accessory.

The instructor will push the footplate out to a point that is just within reach of the client’s leg length. Affix feet to the footplate so that we achieve an approximate hip width position. This will ensure that the ankles, knees, and hips are aligned or “stacked.”  Feet should be parallel. Exceptions to this suggested setup would be subjects with larger frames or those that may lack internal rotation of the femur at the hip. In either case it may be optimal to take a wider stance with the toes angled out slightly. This will help to minimize abdominal compression at the lower turnaround and will account for the lack of rotation at the hip. Importantly, the knees should then track out over the feet at that same approximate angle.

The instructor can carefully release the control of the footplate to the client who will have their feet in place. There will be a total of 38 pounds (20 from the main and 18 from the accessory) pushing back against the client, which will make it easier for the client to keep their feet in place. At this point the instructor will show the client how to place

Adjust seat to allow footplate to abut end stop just before knees fully straighten. It is advisable to push the seat in a couple of settings closer than what appears necessary to account for the spacing that is created under load (note: this only applies to the first time on the machine during the setup).

Bring footplate back to establish starting point (lower turnaround) taking note of the gap. Consider the knee bend and hip flexion for each individual client. Also note that the instructor will have to assist the unloaded footplate back as the client will most likely not be able to flex their hips enough to get the footplate into the starting position we desire (note: this only applies to the first time on the machine during the setup).

When the footplate is at the desired position for the lower turnaround (and starting position), the instructor may ask the client to pin the weight stack at the suggested weight so as not to reach across the client’s body. In the event that the trainer has long enough arms and/or the weight is light enough that the higher plates can be reached more easily, the trainer can just pin the weight themselves. This would be the ideal scenario and note will only happen on the initial setup of the machine.

The instructor must take into consideration that when the movement is loaded, the resulting compression of the padding and flexing of the movement arms will create more space than was apparent without loading.
Posture/Get Set:
Chest up - lay back in the seat with head forward or supported by a pillow. Hands on either set of handles. Face and jaw relaxed, breathing freely.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

LOAD UP:  From the starting position (lower turn), keeping neutral head position (cue to get into position with something along the lines of “chin down”), establish breathing then gradually apply pressure through the footplate. Inform the subject to notice the counter pressure that goes through the hips and lower back into the back pad.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “perfect” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

CONCENTRIC:  Subject will move smoothly through the concentric touch and go at end stop, with the “click” at the moment that happens (or wherever strength and effort permit movement near the end of a set). There is no pause at any point on a Leg Press.
ECCENTRIC:  After the load up and first concentric, and immediately after the click at the upper turn, the instructor may cue “ease out…do not speed up.”

LOWER TURN:  While the client is in the first eccentric phase of the set, the instructor must inform the client of what will constitute the lower turnaround and what the client is expected to do there. In this case the client will “touch and go” or “be continuous at the bottom” or “barely touch, barely start” or “seamlessly change direction as the weights touch” or “soft touch, do not pause.”  All of those cues require the client to control their pace and increase their focus as they sense for the exact moment the weights touch. Again, this creates a level of safety we require with our Continuous Tension protocol. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.
Keep hips down. Do not allow the pelvis to roll up and/or tailbone to lift out of the seat.
One continuous pace with no perceivable pause at any point until concentric movement stalls.

Maintain posture, head position, pace, and knee path throughout. Knees should track through the same path concentrically and eccentrically, to ensure consistent loading of target musculature and to keep the ankles, knees, and hips “stacked.”

And while we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.

It may be necessary or beneficial to describe “gradual” to the subject (e.g. 20 pounds of pressure, 40 pounds, 60 pounds, eventually reaching enough force to begin moving). Or have client imagine that there was 100 pounds on weight stack and they are to gradually find 101 pounds of pressure, or just enough to crack the weight stack. Also remind them that this gradual load up may take 3 to 5 seconds before movement actually occurs.
There is no pause on a leg press. It is one continuous effort. Care should still be given to exaggerate control on the changes of direction (“drag out the turn” or “almost pause but don’t”).

If a clients’ feet slide up the footplate or the torso shifts up into shoulder pads, be attentive to ensure knees cannot lock out at upper turnaround (end stop). If so, give a verbal cue and properly timed click to prevent a fully straightened knee. Inform the client of this temporary change and consider adjusting settings for subsequent sets.

In general, a higher foot position will decrease knee flexion and increase hip flexion, resulting in a more glute biased movement. A lower foot position will increase knee flexion and create more quad biased movement. Both muscle groups will contribute to some degree however in either scenario.

As has been discussed throughout the Academy, it is imperative that the MSF Exercise Practitioner become keenly aware of how much intensity to provide each individual client on every exercise in each workout. So it will be in their best interest to introduce the concept of resistance training more conservatively. Start lighter and teach them how to control the movement. They’ll be better able to receive instruction when they’re not overwhelmed by the struggle. We still absolutely need to teach them intensity and progress their effort but it will be a slower, longer process for these types. Again, show the client that we care more about their workout than they do! See more discussion on the progression of quality and effort in the point below.

Further considerations for achieving a more glute biased setup on the Leg Press:

In general, if we want to feel/use the glutes more, we would want to increase hip flexion and decrease knee flexion. So a more upright seat back is going to accomplish this. P2 would be “more glutes” theoretically than P3.
In addition, raising the feet on the platform would act to decrease knee flexion, which would also make it "more glutes" theoretically.

We say ‘theoretically’ here because at the end of the day, some folks just aren't going to feel their glutes working no matter what and that's not uncommon particularly for that muscle group. But the glutes are still working given the movement pattern.

Anytime we have a more upright position, there will be more hip flexion, which means there is also more spinal flexion, especially on the LP. For some folks (i.e. spines) it may rise to a point where it is not tolerable. In this case we would look to increase their gap, so it would make for a shallower lower turnaround. But this is at odds with us wanting more hip flexion in the first place to bias the glutes. However, if it is bothering the low back, we have to fix that first.

While we often structure client's workouts with Lumbar either first or second in the sequence, it is advisable to try and put as much space between it and the LP. In fact, in cases where the client has a sensitive lower back, it may be best to pair the Lumbar with the Leg Extension and avoid the LP in the same workout. Not because it is inherently dangerous, but there is a chance that the fatigue, or more specifically the "pump", felt from the Lumbar may be carried through to the LP where the spinal flexion will only exacerbate it. If you’ve ever experienced this, you’ll know it is very uncomfortable. But if we are going to include the Lumbar in the same workout as the LP (and again, that's totally acceptable), just make sure there are a few exercises in between to allow time for the pump to dissipate.
It may be that the client cannot tolerate P2 at all and that is fine. It simply means we are going to have to use P3 and lose a little bit of the glute biasing advantage that P2 affords us.

Another consideration would be to perform ABD directly into LP to create a bit of a prefatigued situation for the glutes. Even though they will be different fibers to some degree because they are different movement patterns, there will still be fatigue in the glute region that may help the client feel the glutes more on the LP.

Considerations for setup:

If the accessory weight stack has weight that either needs to be cleared or set, that must be done prior to having the client sit. Once the accessory stack is set, the instructor will move the movement arm (carriage) of the machine all the way back and place the selector pin into the main stack to lock the movement arm in place.

Determine height of the seat pad, by approximating the iliac crest of the subject with the level of the roller pad at the back of the seat. This is the theoretical alignment for this exercise. In theory, this will optimally align the axis of rotation of the machine with the axis of rotation of the body, the top of the pelvis. See the following point for the practical alignment considerations.

From a practical standpoint, the instructor should still take into consideration the length of the spine and/or the relative size of the hip girdle and surrounding tissues. In either case, there is a possibility where there will be a substantial shift in the center of gravity, giving the subject more mass above the movement arm of the machine. They become more “top heavy” in a sense. This will create additional leverage that does not come from the targeted musculature and can lead to a false sense of progression. As a result, there is a likelihood that the subject will require more weight, simultaneously making the exercise less effective with more risk.

With this practical consideration in mind, have the subject sit upright in the seat while moving the back pad (movement arm) up against the upper back. The pad should make contact with a majority of the shoulder blade area.
If the back pad is under the shoulder blades, the seat is too high.
If the back pad is near or making contact with the cervical spine, the seat is too low.
Both the theoretical and practical alignment considerations should be used in setting the seat.

The next consideration is the footplate setting. In order to move the footplate closer to the subject, the femur restraint (knee pad) must first be raised and moved in to approximate the position over the knees. This will allow room for the footplate to be moved into the desired position.

Once the feet are on the footplate, it is best to fasten the seatbelt across the crease of the hip. If the seatbelt is applied before the feet are up, there may be difficulty in lifting the legs. And if the seatbelt is applied after the footplate and femur restraint have been set, there may be too much abdominal congestion for proper placement.

The footplate should be located so that when the feet are placed on the platform the knee joint is slightly higher than the hip joint, resulting in a slight downward angle of the femur toward the subject. (NOTE: In many cases it helps to picture the bones of the subject when aligning rather than just the limb in its entirety. This is one such example where the instructor should try and estimate the position of the femur itself when evaluating the relationship of the knee height to the hip).

With the footplate setting established, the femur restraint should be positioned and tightened down so that the pads basically straddle the knees evenly (i.e. the patella should be approximately centered in the opening between the two pad, with one pad sitting above the knee on the femur and the other resting below the knee along the tibia).

The pads should be snug enough to allow a little bit of wiggle room against the leg but not enough that there is a space or gap. Additionally, the angle of the pads, which is fixed, should be as congruent as possible to the angle of the knee in order to create a secure lock.

If the pads of the femur restraint are not at least close to congruent to the knee angle, then the placement of the foot on the footplate needs to be adjusted. Oftentimes the knee angle is too severe and will need to be opened. For most, this means they will probably have to raise the foot closer to the top of the footplate. Keep in mind this may affect the knee height/femur slope so the footplate may have to be adjusted as well.

With the lower body secure, the next step will be to determine the lower turnaround (and starting point) for the exercise. The instructor will grab the movement arm and remove the main stack selector pin and carefully pull the movement arm (and the client) forward into the desired flexion.

Ideally there will be a standardized gap for the lower turnaround for most subjects. But as noted above, there needs to be a consideration made for the size and tolerance of each individual. A larger subject or one with a history of low back issues will likely have a larger gap resulting in less flexion at the lower turnaround.

There should always be a conservative approach to setting the lower turnaround on the lumbar exercise and this setting should be made with an abundance of caution. There is an increased risk with this movement pattern especially when under load in spinal flexion. Additionally, most of the benefits are attributable to the extension pattern of the movement.

Once the subject has been brought to the starting point, there may have been some shifting back in the seat that would require an adjustment of the femur pads by giving an additional crank to make snug again.
Posture/Get Set:

The cue to begin the lumbar exercise would be something to the effect of, “chin tucked, chest up, establish your breathing and gradually begin to build pressure into the back pad by lifting the ribcage.”

Instinctively, there will likely be an urge to lift the chin and throw the head back along with a valsalva breath hold timed with sudden application of force. Our instruction should prevent this. Give the instruction slowly, directly, and clearly so that it may be processed and implemented.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

LOAD UP: Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the gradual load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “perfect” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

Even if the client has properly prevented lifting the chin on the load up, there will still tend to be an urge to throw the head back in the contracted/extended position. This poses a risk to the neck and contributes to the extension effort creating a false sense of progress. In other words, the weight of the head makes it easier to reach the end stop, taking away from the desired work of the lumbar muscles.

The trainer should also be attentive to the possibility of an emphasized leg drive under loose pads or in situations where the knees are NOT higher than the hips. This is an incorrect setting and should be reevaluated. In this case, the movement then becomes more of a hip extension than a true lumbar extension.

CONCENTRIC: As the client makes their way through the concentric portion of the first rep, it is helpful to describe the anatomical action that is expected. Something along the lines of “chest up, back arched…” or “lift your chest and arch your back” seem to work well here. Also note, that these two cues essentially accomplish the same thing, spinal extension. But the different phrasing may resonate more clearly for some so this is our attempt to be descriptive while keeping our language simple. Most clients will NOT know how to “extend their spine” or how to “squeeze” their lower back.

UPPER TURN: As the subject approaches the upper turnaround (end stop), the instructor should watch intently to assess their range of motion and tolerance of the extension pattern. If the subject can tolerate the full extension permitted by the machine the instructor should ensure that the full range of motion has in fact been achieved. This will allow for more accurate record keeping and a more conservative progression.

At the instance the subject reaches the end stop there should be a brief pause in the contracted position (and a 2 to 3 second “squeeze” from the third rep on). This is unlike our compound pushing movements (LP, CP, OH, SD) where the upper turnaround is met with continuous change of direction into the eccentric phase. This brief pause and slightly longer squeeze require an additional level of focus and control, making the movement safer. They also afford the subject an opportunity to “feel” the target muscles.

Verbiage on a squeeze might be “keep arching, keep breathing, [click], ease out.”  Keep in mind we need to teach the client HOW to squeeze. Saying “squeeze” alone is not a useful instruction. The MSF Exercise Practitioner is constantly teaching!

ECCENTRIC: Once the desired duration is achieved in the contracted position (either brief pause of 1 second or slightly longer squeeze of 2 to 3 seconds), the instructor will click at that exact moment. The click is immediately followed with the instruction to “ease out, and do not speed up” or something to that effect. This is the first repetition and the instructor is setting expectations for the entire set.

LOWER TURN: Now that the client is in the first eccentric phase of the set, the instructor must inform the client of what will constitute the lower turnaround and what the client is expected to do there. In this case the client will “touch and go” or “be continuous at the bottom” or “barely touch, barely start” or “seamlessly change direction as the weights touch” or “soft touch, do not pause.”  All of those cues require the client to control their pace and increase their focus as they sense for the exact moment the weights touch. Again, this creates a level of safety we require with our Continuous Tension protocol. Remember there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.

Because of the series of restraints on this exercise (seat belt, femur restraint, movement arm), control of the posture and path are essentially forced. Reminders to control the head position and to arch the back are helpful but otherwise those 2 P’s are accounted for. The most important reminder here will be to maintain a controlled pace.

And while we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.

But of paramount importance is the fact that the lumbar exercise should NEVER be taken to failure. There is a greater likelihood that the subject will change their behavior/execution as a result of the increasing perceived exertion. Stay within the tolerable limit of each individual client, making sure that every rep is able to be completed with exacting control.
NOTES

It is our company policy that we ascertain any and all limitations and/or contraindications to resistance training for all of our clients and determine which movement patterns these may affect. This is one of the primary purposes of having the prospective client complete the consultation paperwork. It is also a primary purpose of the consultation itself, to understand the limitations of each individual and to tailor the workouts accordingly. There will be certain subjects that do not tolerate lumbar extension from an orthopedic standpoint. For these individuals it may make sense to omit the lumbar movement pattern altogether until they have medical clearance or a better understanding of the diagnosis if they do not already have one.

While avoiding the movement pattern altogether would be the most conservative approach overall, we may be able to actually help the client by strengthening the area. For those with no underlying orthopedic issue, the most conservative approach would be to perform a Timed Static Contraction (TSC). In this situation, the instructor would pin a heavy enough weight so that the movement arm cannot be moved (i.e. too heavy to actually lift). Then, with the client properly secured in the seat, the instructor will position the movement arm to some approximate midpoint in the range of motion, maybe slightly biased toward the upper turnaround. The instructor would then lead the client through an increasing STATIC effort against the back pad. This is typically a 50% effort for 30 seconds, a 75% effort for another 30 seconds, and a final 30 seconds at an all out effort, for a total of 90 seconds of continuous effort. This approach when followed at least weekly for months at a time can build an appreciable level of strength contributing to improved function of the lower back muscles. There also tends to be a carryover effect to what has been estimated at 15 degrees in either direction of the position of the static exercise. There is also a possibility that the client will be able to one day perform the lumbar exercise dynamically and continue to progress.

In the course of regular use of the Lumbar Extension machine, the instructor may observe what appears to be inconsistency in a client’s performance. This can certainly happen on any exercise and tends to be encountered more frequently for those that are less coordinated or more intensity adverse. But for the Lumbar Extension specifically, this can be due in part to the variability in the setup. The instructor should be attentive to the idea that slight differences in the footplate location, tightness of the femur restraint, and tightness of the seat belt can all contribute to making the exercise harder or easier. In some instances the client may not be able to achieve a full range of motion with a weight that they have been able to in previous workouts. Just be aware that the variation in setup can be a reason and that the instructor should strive to be as consistent as possible.

There will also be instances when the subject finds the pressure from the roller pad at the pack of the seat uncomfortable. In this case there are a few things to consider. The first would be to check and see if the subject is wearing a belt, which can cause additional pressure. Or having the knee too high relative to the hip will create more of a horizontal force pushing the femur back into the hip, which is then pushed back into the roller. So consider letting the footplate out slightly to lower the knee. The last consideration would be to either raise or lower the seat to change the contact point of the roller pad on the body. This is another example of practical alignment. Any “fine tuning” necessary to make the movement tolerable for the client needs to be documented in the settings on the chart so that we may be consistent going forward.

Considerations for setup:

Because the seat is higher off the ground than some of the other machines, most clients will require a stool to support the legs. Some may need a stool for entry so be attentive to this need and proactively guide them in safely.
There is a standard gap of 2 on the weight stack to which we are basing the seat setting.

Determine height of the seat by having the client sit with arms hanging straight down by their sides. Then have them bend only at the elbow to raise the hands up and just in front of the torso. The handles should intersect with and rest in the hand at this position in the lower turnaround.

Subjects with a compromised shoulder joint may benefit from having a lower seat and/or a larger gap of the weight stack. This will shorten the range of motion in the bottom part of the movement, which may make the exercise more tolerable orthopedically.
Subject will place the hands near the bottom of the handles resulting in a neutral grip. This tends to be the most joint friendly hand position for most exercises.

Note the angle of the handle in the starting position of the movement. It is not parallel with the floor or level, but rather angled down. This would indicate that a forward pressure at a right angle to the handle is required for proper leverage. This will dictate a slight outward angle of the elbow to better align the forearm with the trajectory of the movement arm. The movement arm travels out and up in a circular or arcing fashion.

Because of the articulation and path of the movement arm this exercise lends itself to a posterior pelvic tilt (PPT). Keeping the abdomen contracted will also add stability to the torso creating an element of protection for the lower back while lifting overhead.

The instructor must take into consideration that when the movement is loaded, the resulting compression of the padding and flexing of the movement arms will create more space than was apparent without loading.
Posture/Get Set:

This exercise utilizes a PPT which requires a contracted abdomen that leads to a rounded back posture. Most subjects will instinctively sit with their chest up and back arched. Care should be taken to explain the posterior tilt and the benefits it provides through abdominal stimulation and safety. One should always consider the required posture as an integral component of the exercise itself.
Because of the PPT required, a neutral head position will have the subject gazing downward toward the floor more so than straight ahead.
Hands are placed near the ends of the handles with palms facing (neutral). Consider hand pads if necessary to blunt the pressure.

The upper arm will approximate the scapular plane, so neither directly in front (sagittal plane) nor out to the side (frontal plane) but rather angled somewhere between 30 to 40 degrees anterior to the frontal plane (scapular plane). The scapulae should be free to find their own natural position, neither forced into retraction or protraction.

The feet should be in contact with a stool so that the legs are not left to dangle. Otherwise there will be an inability to properly maintain posture and there will be a loss of output and stability. Not to mention that many subjects will find this uncomfortable and distracting. The more someone is given an opportunity to move, shift, or wiggle, the less effective the exercise will be and there is an additional element of risk.
The movement will begin at the lower turnaround.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

From the starting position (lower turn), hips back, feet supported, hands near ends of the handles, upper arm aligning to the scapular plane (elbows pointed out 30 to 40 degrees from frontal plane), activating the PPT, chin tucked slightly in neutral head position, establish breathing then gradually apply pressure through the heel of the palms.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “perfect” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

Importantly, the initial force to begin the movement will require a slight horizontal component creating a vector perpendicular to the angled handle. While the exercise is categorized as a ‘vertical push’ it is not purely vertical.
Maintain PPT throughout, neutral head position, and arm path. Elbows should track through the same path concentrically and eccentrically, to ensure consistent loading of target musculature.

Ideally, the arms should entirely straighten in the upper turnaround allowing for some scapular elevation. While there should not necessarily be a deliberate shrug in the overhead position, there will be some natural elevation as part of the scapulohumeral rhythm.

The instructor should stay attentive to the range of motion and let the full movement happen in order to properly time the click. Again as has been a similar theme to a lot of the exercises, there is one and only one moment that makes sense for the click. The subject should also be aware that the click will come only after the full range of motion has been achieved on each rep (or wherever strength and effort permit movement near the end of a set).

After the load up and first concentric, and immediately after the click, the instructor may cue “ease out and do not speed up.”  Then the instructor needs to establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround of the set, which on a chest press will be to “touch and go” or “be continuous” or “do not pause”. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.
One continuous pace with no perceivable pause at any point until concentric movement stalls.
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and arm path, and throughout. Elbows should track through the same path concentrically and eccentrically, to ensure consistent loading of target musculature.

And while we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.

It may be necessary or beneficial to describe “gradual” to the subject (e.g. 20 pounds of pressure, 40 pounds, 60 pounds, eventually reaching enough force to begin moving). Or have client imagine that there was 100 pounds on weight stack and they are to gradually find 101 pounds of pressure, or just enough to crack the weight stack. Also remind them that this gradual load up may take 3 to 5 seconds before movement actually occurs.

There is no pause on an overhead press. It is one continuous effort. Care should still be given to exaggerate control on the changes of direction (“drag out the turn” or “almost pause but don’t”). Also make sure the subject reaches the upper turnaround by fully straightening the arms prior to the click that indicates the change of direction. New instructors tend to click too soon causing confusion on exactly where the change of direction occurs and a truncated movement.

Height of the client and arm length will be a primary driver of the seat setting. Taller subjects will usually have a lower seat and there may even be a need to increase the gap from the standard setting of two to maintain favorable joint angles.

In the event that the subject experiences shoulder pain/discomfort in the upper half of the movement, then shortening the range of motion somewhere near the midpoint of the concentric can make the exercise more tolerable. A selector pin can be placed into the stack pin to create a hard end stop so that a consistent range of motion can be used.

Importantly, while learning the Continuous Tension protocol, the subject will most likely be using a relatively light weight and as a result will probably be capable of performing a higher number of reps, spending more time on the machine. While this may seem conducive to learning, it can also be counterproductive from a discomfort standpoint. Yes a big part of the learning curve is to be able to produce an effort while managing discomfort, but there can be diminishing returns in that the movement becomes intolerable before it is stimulative. Ideally we should be striving for perfect form with “faster” reps (i.e. 6 second positive, 6 second negative) and a “heavier” weight that leads to failure in 10 or fewer reps. While this may not be achievable or advisable in the initial sessions, as long as the subject is demonstrating a clear understanding of the control required, we may progress the intensity more quickly.

Considerations for setup:

Because the seat is higher off the ground than other machines, most clients will require a stool to support the legs. Some may need a stool for entry so be attentive to this need and proactively guide them in safely. A lower seat position may be required for those that need assistance or maybe shorter than average. If this is the case, we should also expect a larger gap to bring the handles further down to meet them. Try to avoid using the 4 highest/furthest from the floor seat positions (avoid 1-4).

The Pulldown exercise is performed with a supinated grip and the handles set so that they are pointing in toward each other and slightly forward (one notch toward neutral). The Torso Arm variation will have a neutral grip and the handles pointing forward, parallel to each other (the neutral grip will only be used selectively, see NOTES section below).

Look to position the back pad so that when sitting upright, the vertical path of the handles is out in front of the subject as opposed to directly in line with them (i.e. the subject should be behind the path of the handles by at least the length of the upper arm). Most will have a back pad setting of 2 or 3, larger subjects may need to sit further back on the seat, so a setting of 1 may be advised.

If the subject is short, lacks mobility, or is severely deconditioned, we will want to lower the seat to make entry/exit a safer process (use seats 5-9). In this case, we will most likely need to increase the gap on the weight stack thereby lowering the handles to be within the subject’s reach.
With a seat of 5 or lower (i.e. closer to the floor) bring the handles down to just within the subject’s reach and pin the weight stack to establish the position of the lower turnaround.
If the weight stack does in fact touch “too soon” (i.e. excessive bend in the elbow) while the client is lowering the weight, consider a lower seat or decreasing the gap.

The ideal grip will have the hands no wider than shoulder width apart. Slightly narrower than shoulder width may even be better considering that a narrow arm path is optimal to better leverage the lats (in the sagittal plane). This will keep the elbows closer to the torso and will help prevent more of a row where the elbows are pulled beyond the torso using the upper back at the expense of the lats.
Posture/Get Set:

Chest up, hips back, chin slightly tucked (neutral), upper back against the top of the seat back, seat belt tightly secured. Because of the seat belt on this exercise it is not necessary to also have a stool. However, some clients may either have trouble getting into the seat without one and/or may find that having their legs dangle is uncomfortable or distracting. As such there should be a stool available either under the seat or off to the side in front of the weight stack. (NOTE: As with anything we do in our role as a professional Exercise Practitioner, we have to be attentive and proactive to the needs of our clients. Using a stool to get into a machine is a perfect example. It should not be up to the client to ask for one, we should anticipate the need and preemptively resolve the issue).

The client and the trainer will pull the handles down together near the contracted position. The loads tend to be heavier on this exercise so the client has to be able to reach the handles and assist. Unlike the compound row however, which requires scapular retraction, the pulldown does not, so the transfer can take place in a stronger position for the client. This tends to be right around eye level.

The trainer will then gradually transfer the weight to the client (i.e. handoff) while giving the verbal indicator “that is yours,” or something to that effect. The client needs to hold the movement arm still to establish control before beginning the eccentric. If there is movement during the handoff the trainer should not yet fully transfer the load. Instruct the client to “increase your force” or “pull harder.”
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

The movement requires an instructor assist as the set will start near the contracted position, with the handles at about eye level. After an accurate handoff, the instructor will cue the client to “slowly begin to let the arms straighten,” or “with control, slowly allow the movement arm to rise.”  Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of any exercise.

LOWER TURNAROUND: Just before the subject’s arms fully straighten and as the plates touch, the subject will “immediately” or “continuously” or “seamlessly” begin bending them again. (Importantly, ‘immediate’ means right away, but does not mean suddenly in this case). But it may also help to have the arms fully straighten just before the weights touch for those subjects that may benefit from a full lengthening/stretch of the torso and arms.

UPPER TURNAROUND: The upper turnaround will be when the subject has drawn the handles down to just under the level of their chin. This will have the humerus aligned with the side of their torso, which is the most contracted position for the lats. And importantly, the wrists can remain flat or straight relative to the forearm in this position, thus minimizing wrist flexion and the limiting discomfort that results.

PULLDOWN VARIATION: As a variation on the pulldown, we may instruct the client to incorporate an abdominal contraction along the way during the concentric, resulting in a fully contracted abdomen at the upper turnaround (remember, the upper turn is a reference to the position of the weight stack, not the limbs of the body). The wrists should still remain straight and the upper arm still aligns with the side of the torso. The arms DO NOT pull the handles further down and the elbows DO NOT  travel further back. It is a subtle and compact abdominal contraction that blends seamlessly into the movement. If this additional component cannot be mastered, it is not worth incorporating and the ribcage should be held still with the hands stopping just below chin level. There is still tremendous benefit to the exercise performed as a pulldown for the lats.

Most subjects will assume that they should pull the handles down and back as far as they can, lifting the weights higher. The instructor should remind them of the real objective to focus on the optimal range of motion for the muscles being targeted.

The trainer will click only after they have visually confirmed that the desirable range of motion has been achieved and the movement has temporarily ceased (i.e. no further contraction is possible or they have arrived at the upper turn). The instructor needs to be attentive to the likelihood that the client will assume that the movement should continue until they hear the click. This is especially true on the Pulldown because the concentric portion will terminate with the handles just below the chin. The client will invariably continue to pull down and back, flexing the wrists more and more to keep the machine moving because they have not yet heard the click. But the click will ONLY come when the proper range of motion has been achieved and the client has established control (brief pause just below chin level). So these two objectives are at odds and the instructor needs to anticipate and be assertive to control the outcome. This will be yet another example of how the trainer cares more about the workout than the client does.

Verbiage used on the concentric might be to “keeping your ribcage still, draw the elbows down and into your sides” or as an extended cue “drive the elbows down into the sides of your ribcage…mmm, hmm…there…[click], ease out, keep that pace.”
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and arm path, and throughout. Elbows should track through the same path concentrically and eccentrically, to ensure consistent loading of target musculature.

INTENSITY: By definition, the set will end when concentric failure is reached (i.e. subject can no longer lift the weight with perfect form). This is where we would note the reps and record only the full reps achieved on the chart. But as discussed throughout the Academy, certain exercises lend themselves to performing additional, partial repetitions and the Pulldown is one of these movements. Especially when the client is able to perform those partial reps beyond the midpoint and with perfect form. Of even more importance for the consideration of training beyond concentric failure (i.e. using partial repetitions) would be the experience and tolerance of the individual. A newer, more deconditioned client would not yet be ready for this more advanced technique. They can simply perform full repetitions to a point where they begin to fatigue and the effort will probably be enough to provide the desired stimulus. Of course we are always attempting to progress every client’s understanding of effort and intensity while improving their quality from session to session as is illustrated in the point below.

While we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.

PULLDOWN vs. TORSO ARM: For the Torso Arm variation of the exercise where the handles point forward and the palms are facing in a neutral grip, essentially everything is the same setup and execution-wise (note: there is no intentional abdominal contraction as is acceptable in the Pulldown). The subject will keep their head and ribcage still and the elbows are pulled into the side of the torso. The major difference is the movement plane the exercise takes place in. The Torso Arm exercise occurs in the frontal plane (an imaginary plane that bisects the body from front to back), whereas the Pulldown occurs in the sagittal plane (bisecting the body between left and right, so arms out in front of the body). With these different movement planes, there is a slightly different bias to the same muscle groups. For instance, the Pulldown will bias the thoracic (upper) and lumbar (middle) divisions of the lats while the Torso Arm will bias the iliac (lower) division of the lats. But both variations will target the lats in an overall fashion especially for more novice trainers. In most cases, there really is no need to specialize or incorporate both movement patterns in an effort to isolate all regions.

SCAPULOHUMERAL RHYTHM: As an aside, it has become customary to want to over correct any sort of scapular movement on overhead or rowing movements. To instruct the subject to essentially pin down the shoulder blades during exercise and to not allow them to move. In keeping with the principles of physiology however, this can establish faulty movement patterns as it obviates the scapulohumeral rhythm specific to the shoulder joint. See the following link in the Muscle & Motion app for further clarity (https://app.strength.muscleandmotion.com/theory-video/104). In simple terms, as the arms are raised overhead, the scapulae rotate upward and elevate to support the shoulder joint. This movement is necessary to accommodate stability at the base of what is essentially a long, movable lever of the arm. If we do in fact just allow the shoulder blades to move freely in the eccentric phase, we should see that they do in fact “find their optimal position” during the concentric phase of the exercise. Unless the subject is egregiously shrugging throughout the movement, do not call attention to the shoulder blades at all, just let them perform their function naturally. It is far more important to stabilize the head and ribcage (posture), establish a consistent arm path and range of motion, and maintain a consistent pace.

The handles should just be within reach while unloaded so that the client can assist the trainer (and vice versa) into the contracted position during the load up. The client can then set the weight down without assistance to unload at the end of the set.

There will be some clients that have a valgus elbow characterized by an abnormal outward angle of the forearm relative to the humerus. In more severe cases, movement at the elbow (often on the eccentric) will result in varying degrees of discomfort. A shortened range of motion that limits elbow extension (larger gap) may be beneficial or performing a pushing movement first can help. If either of those strategies do not alleviate the issue, it may be beneficial to try the neutral handles (Torso Arm) setup.

Considerations for setup:
There are several considerations when establishing the settings for a client on the Pullover, along with the need to satisfy Theoretical versus Practical alignment.

The seat back has two options, up and back or down and forward. Most clients will need the extra space afforded by the up and back position. Smaller framed individuals may benefit from having the backpad in the forward position but this will likely only be a handful of clients.
Determine the seat height by first taking into account the height of the subject. Taller subjects will most likely have a lower seat, shorter subjects will have a higher seat.

As a rotary movement, the Pullover has a single axis of rotation and in theory, this axis is to be aligned with the axis of rotation of the body, the shoulder joint. But because the shoulder joint will naturally travel or move off of its axis during this movement (and most movements) we will need to consider the approximate middle position of the joint’s excursion to achieve the best fit.
This will entail starting with a seat height that has the axis of rotation of the machine slightly above the center of the shoulder joint while client is seated with arms at their sides.

The next consideration is the position of the arm pads which have an option for wide (W), middle (M), or narrow (N) settings. Most clients will likely have the pads in the middle setting. This will be based on the width of the client's shoulders and torso. Ideally the upper arms should travel as close to the sides of the torso as possible as this will create the best leverage for the lats. Keep in mind that the narrower the setting, the more care must be given when bringing the movement arm down into place as the client will have to maneuver themselves between the pads.

The lower turnaround will be set with a gap, which for most clients can be standardized at 6. The instructor will still evaluate this ROM for every single client as safety has to be the priority. If after handing off the movement arm to perform the eccentric of the first rep, the instructor anticipates that the ROM will be excessive, the instructor should take control of the movement arm and reassess.

With the settings established, the instructor still needs to consider the practical alignment that allows the elbow to “land” at least halfway down along the arm pads. Additionally the elbow should be bent at around 90 degrees and should be able to stay in that same position throughout the full range of motion of the exercise without any sliding of the upper arm along the pads. If there is sliding or the elbows are forced to bend or straighten more, then a further adjustment is required.
Posture/Get Set:

This exercise utilizes a PPT which requires a contracted abdomen that leads to a rounded back posture. Most subjects will instinctively sit with their chest up and back arched. Clients will also instinctively push down on the movement arm with their hands/arms. Neither of these instinctive measures are correct, however, and care should be taken to explain the posterior pelvic tilt and the purpose of the elbow pads over using the hands. One should always consider the required posture and the details of the execution as an integral component of the exercise itself.

The trainer will methodically pull the movement arm down, over top of the client, into the contracted position. Attentive care must be given to ensure that the client can maneuver their arms between the elbow pads as those are set as narrow as possible to approximate the sides of the ribcage.
It is also advisable for the instructor to grab the movement arm further out/up from the axis so they can better leverage their strength to gain control.

The trainer will then gradually transfer the weight to the client (i.e. handoff) while giving the verbal indicator “driving back through your elbow, tighten your abdomen, that…is…yours,” or something to that effect. The client needs to briefly keep the movement arm still to establish control before beginning the eccentric. If there is movement during the handoff the trainer should not yet fully transfer the load. Instruct the client to “increase your force” or “push harder.”
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

The movement requires an instructor assist as the set will start in the contracted position (upper turn). The PPT and effort through the elbows while contracting will remind them of the feeling we are seeking. After a proper handoff, the instructor will cue the client to “slowly begin to allow the movement arm to rise…keeping the pressure through the elbows.”  Remember there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of every exercise.

Once the movement arm is raised far enough (weight is being lowered), they will “continuously” or “seamlessly” or “immediately” touch and go by tightening the abdomen, leveraging through the seat belt, and driving through the elbows. (Importantly, ‘immediate’ means right away, but does not mean suddenly in this case).
The upper turnaround (squeeze) will be when the subject has fully contracted their lats by drawing the elbows down into the sides of the torso and tightening the midsection.

Most subjects will assume that they should push the movement arm down/back as far as they can to lift the weights higher. The instructor should remind them of the real objective to focus on the optimal range of motion for the muscles being targeted.

So these two objectives are at odds and the instructor needs to anticipate and be assertive to control the outcome. This will be yet another example of how the trainer cares more about the workout than the client does.
Verbiage used on the concentric might be to “draw the elbows down into the ribs.”

Important to note here, this is one of the few exercises where the posture changes between rep phases. In the eccentric, as the arms are raising, the ribcage will naturally rise into an anterior pelvic tilt. On the concentric, the abdomen will tighten, which will draw the ribcage down.

Due to potential variability in the manufacturing and/or installation processes, the standard gap on this exercise should be determined specifically for each individual machine. This is covered as part of the normal onboarding process but is emphasized here as another measure of safety.

In the event that clients are resting in the contracted position, the trainer may choose to use a selector pin to create an end stop near the upper turnaround, which will give a concentric termination point for the client to increase their effort against.

Considerations for setup:

Because the seat is higher off the ground than other machines, all clients will require a stool to support the legs. Some may need a stool for entry so be attentive to this need and proactively guide them in safely. A lower seat position may be required for those that need assistance or maybe shorter than average. If this is the case, we should also expect a larger gap to bring the handles further down to meet them. Try to avoid using the 4 highest/furthest from the floor seat positions (avoid 1-4).

The determination of the seat height will require at least two factors. Firstly, the seat height will determine the lower turnaround and starting position for the movement. Secondly, the seat height will determine the intersection of the hands and the movement arm and the resulting shoulder and elbow angles.

Typically, there will be no gap used on the Seated Dip as the seat height determines the lower turn around. EXCEPTION: In the event that the subject lacks mobility, is severely deconditioned, or is just too short to comfortably get seated, we should opt for a lower/closer to the floor seat setting (seat 5-9). In this case, we will need to gap the weight stack to lower the handles to properly align with the lower seat setting. This will allow the subject to more easily get into and out of the machine and they will be better able to reach the stool when performing the exercise.

Keep in mind we are looking for the upper arm to be angled off the body (abducted) approximately 45 to 60 degrees. The elbow will be bent at approximately 90 degrees or more depending on the mobility and tolerance of the subject. The humerus will likely be behind the torso to some extent in the starting position. This will also be influenced by the back pad setting, which is discussed below. The front or forward most part handles should approximate the hands in this position.

The client will have a choice of either using a neutral hand placement or a pronated hand placement where they “cap” the end of the handle. It is advisable to use a pair of “Fat Gripz” handles to spread the pressure out over a larger area of the palm for a more comfortable grip. Also keep in mind that with a pushing exercise like the Seated Dip, Chest Press, and Overhead Press, the subject is not truly gripping the handle but rather pushing through the heel of the hand/palm.

In the interest of safety, the instructor should always err on a more conservative setting by having the seat higher. If the seat is too low, the shoulder capsule may be overly stretched along with the pecs and the elbow may be hyper flexed. This will also be influenced by the position of the back pad, which is addressed in the points below.

The size of the seat itself and the manner of execution of the Seated Dip exercise lend itself to fine tuning the subject’s ultimate positioning. Smaller subjects may find the need to be slightly more forward in the seat while larger subjects may be further back. Because this exercise is performed with a leaning/rounding forward posture, a larger/longer torso will lean forward more and as a result will likely have to start from further back in the seat to end up in the desired position. The opposite then is true for shorter torsos.
In the event that a subject’s hands feel as though they will slip forward off the handles, it may be remedied by moving forward in the seat some OR moving the hands slightly back on the handles.

The purpose of the back pad is to oppose the reactionary forces of the movement arm by giving leverage to the torso. As such the back pad should be angled forward and lowered down to meet the mid/upper back. When properly set, the back pad will also likely cause the subject to have to lean forward some, resulting in more of a stretch at the chest and shoulder and an increase in elbow flexion. This is why the seat height, back pad, and position on the seat must be considered together when determining the optimal starting point of the exercise for each individual.

The instructor must take into consideration that when the movement is loaded, the resulting compression of the padding, lifting out of the seat and into the belt, and flexing of the movement arms will create more space than was apparent without loading. As such, further adjustments may be warranted.
Posture/Get Set:
Ensure seat back is raised up and out of the way in order to get the subject properly seated.

Chest up, hips back, chin slightly tucked (neutral) with shoulders held in retraction. This will happen naturally as the seat height and back pad will force the posture in a sense, aside from the head position. Upper arms should be abducted (pointed back and out to the sides) somewhere between 45 to 60 degrees and the elbows will be bent 90 degrees or more based on the mobility and tolerance of the subject. The seat belt should be fastened and tightly secured as the reactionary forces will lift the subject out of the seat.
Note: while the get set posture has the chest up and shoulder blades retracted, the movement will finish in a moderate to full protraction as the elbows straighten. See Execution below.
Once seated and belted in place, the seat back is lowered to the desired setting  See setting considerations above.

The feet should be in contact with a stool for added stability and comfort. If the feet are left dangling, there will be an inability to properly maintain position and there will be a loss of output and stability. Not to mention that many subjects will find this uncomfortable and distracting. The more someone is given an opportunity to move, shift, or wiggle, the less effective the exercise will be and there is an additional element of risk.

Hands are placed at or near the ends of the movement arm, preferably on a pair of Fat Gripz handles. The subject will have a choice of either neutral or pronated, with the latter requiring the hands to be placed at the very ends. In some cases a subject may find the hand placement uncomfortable and a slight adjustment is permitted. Consider hand pads too in an effort to blunt the pressure.
The movement will begin at the lower turnaround.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

From the starting position (lower turn), keeping chest up with shoulders in retraction and chin slightly tucked in a neutral head position, upper arms abducted, establish breathing then gradually apply pressure through the heel of the palms.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “mmm, hmm” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive reinforcement.
The subject will have no choice but to leverage off of the back pad but it may be helpful to draw awareness to its use.

The movement arms will travel down below the level of the seat as the client attempts to (1) completely straighten the arms, (2) protract the shoulder blades, and (3) tighten the abdomen. These three components are most easily performed in a blended and synergistic fashion.
There is no end stop on this movement so the instructor must watch intently for those three components to occur and for the movement to cease before clicking. This is the upper turnaround.

Most subjects will assume that they should push the handles down as far as they can, lifting the weights higher. The instructor should remind them of the real objective to focus on fully exhausting the three components of the fully contracted position.

The trainer will click only after they have visually confirmed that the desirable range of motion has been achieved and the movement has temporarily ceased (i.e. no further contraction is possible). The instructor needs to be attentive to the likelihood that the client will assume that the movement should continue until they hear the click. But the opposite is true. The click will ONLY happen when the proper range of motion has been achieved by the client. So these two objectives are at odds and the instructor needs to anticipate and be assertive to control the outcome. This will be yet another example of how the trainer cares more about the workout than the client does.

Verbiage used on the concentric might be to “drive your arms straight, and tighten down hard on the abdominals, keep breathing, [click], ease out” or to “keep straightening, keep breathing, round your back hard into the back pad, [click], ease out.”  Remember, the MSF Exercise Practitioner is always looking to teach clients HOW to properly execute the movements on a path toward mastery. As such, our instruction needs to travel on that path as well.

Once the load up and first concentric have been completed and the instructor clicks to indicate the beginning of the eccentric phase, the instructor then needs to establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround of the set. On a Seated Dip the lower turnaround will be as the weight stack touches and can be cued with something to the effect of, “touch and go” or “be continuous” or “do not pause” or “barely touch, barely start”. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.

One continuous pace with only the briefest pause allowed as the instructor attentively observes the full excursion of the concentric phase before immediately clicking the subject back into the eccentric. This pattern is carried out until concentric movement stalls, which constitutes reaching muscular failure.
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and arm path, and throughout. Elbows should track through the same path concentrically and eccentrically, to ensure consistent loading of target musculature.

And while we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.
NOTES

It may be necessary or beneficial to describe “gradual” to the subject (e.g. 20 pounds of pressure, 40 pounds, 60 pounds, eventually reaching enough force to begin moving). Or have client imagine that there was 100 pounds on weight stack and they are to gradually find 101 pounds of pressure, or just enough to crack the weight stack. Also remind them that this gradual load up may take 3 to 5 seconds before movement actually occurs.

There is no pause on a seated dip. It is one continuous effort. Care should still be given to exaggerate control on the changes of direction (“drag out the turn” or “almost pause but don’t”). Also make sure the subject reaches the fully contracted position (upper turn) prior to the click that indicates the change of direction. New instructors tend to click too soon causing confusion on exactly where the change of direction occurs.

Importantly, while learning the Continuous Tension protocol, the subject will most likely be using a relatively light weight and as a result will probably be capable of performing a higher number of reps, spending more time on the machine. While this may seem conducive to learning, it can also be counterproductive from a discomfort standpoint. Yes a big part of the learning curve is to be able to produce an effort while managing discomfort, but there can be diminishing returns in that the movement becomes intolerable before it is stimulative. Ideally we should be striving for perfect form with “faster” reps (i.e. 6 second positive, 6 second negative) and a “heavier” weight that leads to failure in 10 or fewer reps. While this may not be achievable or advisable in the initial sessions, as long as the subject is demonstrating a clear understanding of the control required, we may progress the intensity more quickly.

Considerations for setup:
There are several considerations when establishing the settings for a client on the Simple Row, along with the need to satisfy Theoretical versus Practical alignment.

Determine the seat height by first taking into account the height of the subject. Taller subjects will most likely have a lower seat, shorter subjects will have a higher seat. The seat will need to be fine tuned so that the upper arm (humerus) is sloped down slightly from the shoulder to the elbow, when in the starting position. So the humeral head in the shoulder joint would be slightly higher than the elbow. Additionally, the top of the head will end up near the padded “work box” overhead when seated.

The theoretical alignment in this case would have the subject’s shoulders directly under the axes of rotation of the machine. However, what tends to be more important is the resulting location of the elbows in the arm pads and the ability for the pads to stay flush/congruent to the subject’s arms during the execution of the movement. This is the practical alignment that will govern the most optimal settings.

As a result of the need to satisfy the practical alignment, look to position the chest pad so that when sitting upright with arms out in front the elbow will land in at least the middle of the concave pads on the movement arm.

Accordingly, we would expect subjects with longer arms to have the chest pad set further out away from the arm pads. And subjects with shorter arms would have the chest pad set in closer to the arm pads. But the following point must also be taken into consideration.

Aside from arm length, the subject’s torso size is also a factor that needs to be considered. A larger torso/abdomen would automatically position the subject further away from the arm pads. To account for this, we may need to bring the chest pad in closer to the arm pads. And a smaller torso may have the chest pad set further back away from the arm pads.

Importantly, given the juxtaposed situations outlined in the two points above, we need to consider the interplay of arm length AND torso size to find the optimal chest pad setting. Ultimately, the determining factor would be the requirement that the arm pads remain flush against the subject’s humerus/elbow throughout the movement.
Once the seat and chest pad are set, we may need to consider a gap to create more space to accommodate subjects at the starting point/lower turnaround.

And finally, the vertical location of and the hand placement on the handles should be considered. Longer arms may require the handles to be slid up into a higher position so that the elbows land closer to the middle of the arm pads when the arms hang from the handles. Additionally, if the subject finds the hand placement creates difficulty in achieving the external rotation required to perform the movement, then they may be advised to “cap” the ends of the handles so that their palms are facing them. This usually allows for a more comfortable execution of the movement at the shoulder.
Posture/Get Set:
Chest up, hips close to the chest pad so that abdomen is on the pad, chin slightly tucked (neutral), arms inside the pads with hands on handles.
Ideally this exercise will be performed with the abdomen against the chest pad so that the ribcage may be lifted, allowing for more thoracic extension and increasing scapular retraction.
This exercise will start at the lower turnaround with an emphasized, chest up posture. Feet on the floor, possibly on the toe of the shoe for subjects with higher seats and shorter legs.
Execution, Instruction, and Turnarounds:

LOAD UP:  From the starting position (lower turn), keeping chest up, neutral head position, arms in place, establish breathing, and gradually begin to apply pressure by driving out through the elbows.

Once the instructor has given the cue to begin the load up, there should be a quiet moment where the instructor is intently observing the actions. If done properly, a simple “perfect” or “yes, just like that” is an opportunity for positive feedback.

CONCENTRIC/UPPER TURN:  Subject will move through this first concentric phase, lifting their chest and drawing their shoulder blades together until they can no longer contract any further (upper turn). Once the desired duration is achieved in the contracted position (either brief pause of 1 second or slightly longer squeeze of 2 to 3 seconds), the instructor will click at that exact moment.
ECCENTRIC:  The click is immediately followed with the instruction to “ease out,  do not speed up” or something to that effect.

The instructor then needs to establish the expectation for the first lower turnaround of the set, which on a Simple Row will be to “touch and go” or “be continuous” or “seamlessly change directions”. Remember, there is always a cue to give on the first eccentric of an exercise.
LOWER TURN:  Touch and go at the lower turn as if “continuously passing through the bottom.”
Keep chest up by leveraging off of the chest pad with the abdomen.

One continuous pace with only a “brief but definite” pause of about one second in the contracted position of the first two reps and a squeeze of two to three seconds from the third rep on. Keep in mind, we cannot simply rely on the cue of ‘squeeze’ in this situation. That can mean various things to different people. We need to teach them HOW to squeeze.

Verbiage for the pause/squeeze in the contracted position might be “leveraging off your abdomen, lift your chest and draw your shoulder blades together as hard as you can…keep breathing, keep still, [click], ease out, don’t speed up” or “keeping your head still, attempt to wrap your shoulder blades around your spine…there, lock it in place, [click], ease out.”  So during the desired duration of the squeeze in the contracted position, we are providing actionable instruction.
Maintain posture, head position, pace, and contact with the arm pads.

Importantly, the number of reps recorded will only be those that the instructor deems were full reps. So if the client does not reach full contraction of the upper back, that is not a full rep and will not be recorded in the rep count on the chart. But due to the nature of certain exercises, and Simple Row being one of them, it may make sense to continue the set despite the client no longer achieving full range of motion. There will still be stimulative tension experienced on the partial reps as long as they are within the client’s exacting control.

The decision to continue a set after reaching concentric failure is highly individual and should be discussed with a studio Leader or with MSF Corporate. For a brand new client, just completing a handful of full range of motion reps may be enough to introduce the exercise. So in other words, we may not even take them to concentric failure if they are new to strength training or if they are showing signs of adverse discomfort or losing proper form. This is a progressive journey.

While we are encouraging the subject to maintain their pace, they should expect to have to increase their effort over the course of a set. Effort does not remain constant. In order to maintain a given pace with increasing fatigue, effort needs to voluntarily increase as a counter to the fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created.

Be prepared to point out the overhead mechanism on the machine upon every entry/exit, regardless of how many times a subject has used the machine. A simple “watch your head” while pointing out the padded component is required to ensure the subject’s safety.

As with many exercises, we can expect each client to have varying capabilities in terms of range of motion. We should encourage as much of a ROM through scapular retraction and ensure the subject is not leaning back to advance the movement arm. Additionally, the instructor should use the first 2 or 3 reps to determine what each individual subject’s ROM is and use that to determine encouragement of effort and registering full repetitions.

The Simple Row exercise works well in situations where a client may be experiencing an elbow, wrist, or hand issue but we still wish to stimulate the upper back muscles. It also works well for those that need to work on improving their posture and maybe best paired with the pulldown movement. In this case, since the pulldown does not address scapular retraction, we can program the Simple Row as a complement without the concern of fatigued arms or grip strength.

Many subjects will come to us with shoulder issues and may or may not be able to tolerate this movement pattern. While avoiding this exercise altogether would be the most conservative approach overall, we may be able to actually help the client by strengthening the area. For those with no underlying orthopedic issue, the most conservative approach would be to perform a Timed Static Contraction (TSC). In this situation, the instructor would pin a heavy enough weight so that the movement arm cannot be moved (i.e. too heavy to actually lift). Then, with the client properly secured in the seat, the instructor will position the movement arm to some approximate midpoint in the range of motion, maybe slightly biased toward the upper turnaround. The instructor would then lead the client through an increasing STATIC effort against the back pad. This is typically a 50% effort for 30 seconds, a 75% effort for another 30 seconds, and a final 30 seconds at an all out effort, for a total of 90 seconds of continuous effort. This approach when followed at least weekly for months at a time can build an appreciable level of strength contributing to improved function of shoulders. There also tends to be a carryover effect to what has been estimated at 15 degrees in either direction of the position of the static exercise. There is also a possibility that the client will be able to one day perform this exercise dynamically and continue to progress.
